kz4m1g.text: A Saudi OpenAI engineer has been arrested for allegedly planting a hidden recording device in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco offices to secretly record sensitive conversations. The U.S. Department of Justice announced Tuesday that Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, was arrested on October 9 and charged with illegally intercepting oral communications. The DOJ says OpenAI security personnel discovered the recording device on September 30, plugged into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room. According to the DOJ, OpenAI determined that the device had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed around September 28, and contained encrypted data. "On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco," says the DOJ press release. Spy device found in OpenAI executive conference roomSource: DOJ The DOJ says the conference room was regularly used for meetings involving confidential information about OpenAI's proprietary research, product plans, technical capabilities, business relationships, and government engagements. Security camera footage allegedly showed Alfozan near the conference room on multiple occasions, despite not being authorized to attend meetings held there. According to the complaint, Alfozan also used a productivity tool to search for information about OpenAI's offices, meeting rooms, executive locations, and meeting schedules. The complaint also says a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse was used to ask questions about building and concealing recording devices. These included inquiries about creating a continuous audio recorder, modifying Wi-Fi connectivity, improving live listening capabilities, and encrypting an SD card. "The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28," alleges the DOJ. On October 5, surveillance footage allegedly captured Alfozan returning to the conference room and looking behind the television where the device had been installed. The complaint says that on that same day, OpenAI security employees discovered a second, similar recording device inside a bag Alfozan had left unattended in another room. In a statement posted on X, OpenAI said it used its own AI models to investigate the suspicious device and help identify the employee responsible. "We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," OpenAI said. The company said it terminated the employee and referred the incident to the FBI. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI added. If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. lyrkxt.text: A critical heap buffer overflow vulnerability (CVE-2026-39919) in the Ghostscript interpreter and rendering engine could allow remote code execution through specially crafted PDF files. The flaw was discovered on August 23 by researchers at Defiant's platform Wordfence using their Argus AI-powered system. Ghostscript is a PostScript and PDF interpreter that can render PDFs as images, generate thumbnails for previews, and optimize PDF files by compressing embedded images and removing unnecessary font data. When generating a PDF thumbnail, WordPress can use the PHP Imagick extension to call ImageMagick, which launches Ghostscript. A specially crafted PDF file containing a JPEG 2000 image can trigger incorrect handling of low-bit-depth samples and mismatched component resolutions. Using Argus, the researchers developed two exploits for CVE-2026-39919 that force Ghostscript to write 1,024 bytes into a 256-byte buffer, corrupting nearby memory and leading to unauthenticated remote code execution in a WordPress deployment. Wordfence focused on WordPress systems, but notes that the flaw affects any online system running Ghostscript 9.21 through 10.07.1 and is exploitable if the payload is adjusted to the environment. The researchers tested ten Linux environments, including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Alpine, and AlmaLinux, as well as an official WordPress Docker image snapshot, and found that all contained the vulnerable code. Tested environmentsSource: Wordfence The researchers tested two proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits and found that their ability to trigger the vulnerability depended on the target environment. In a lab testbed, they executed the exploits 10,240 times against Linux packages but failed to achieve remote code execution. However, they successfully executed code remotely on a purpose-built test server. The researchers found that modifying the PDF's fonts, language settings, font configuration, and one core system library enabled the exploit to succeed, although not reliably. In WordPress environments specifically, successful exploitation has four prerequisites: An attacker can upload a PDF, anonymously or through a low-privileged account. The site processes that PDF to generate a preview or thumbnail. The processing chain reaches Ghostscript, with the necessary software and policy settings permitting PDF rendering. Ghostscript contains the unpatched vulnerable decoding code. Wordfence noted that stock WordPress does not permit anonymous Media Library uploads. More generally, any application that renders attacker-supplied PDFs through affected Ghostscript code may expose the flaw, and authentication requirements for exploitation depend on the application. Artifex, the maintainer of Ghostscript, rolled out a fix on September 8, in version 10.08.0 of the interpreter. Fixes were also backported to older versions, so users should check the revision details for patch status. WordPress administrators need to ensure, through their hosting provider, that Ghostscript has been upgraded to version 10.08.0 or later. If using Docker, it is recommended to rebuild and redeploy with an updated, patched base image. If unable to upgrade to a fixed Ghostscript release, it is recommended to block PDF uploads to the server or disable PDF rendering in ImageMagick. Wordfence said it has not seen any in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-39919 yet. 13n8bmr.text: Anthropic is warning that small AI models could soon be able to self-replicate across consumer IoT devices, from Android TV boxes to smart ovens, creating distributed botnets capable of running AI workloads without relying on data centers. The company's experiments showed that models could identify unfamiliar devices, connect them into a network, and prepare them to run an AI model. Although the researchers successfully distributed the Gemma4-26B-A4B model from Google DeepMind on 15 off-brand Android TV boxes, they did not demonstrate a fully autonomous, self-replicating AI worm running on real IoT hardware. However, they estimate that smaller models could achieve self-replication by the end of the year if they continue to improve at their historical rate. “Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes,” Anthropic warns. “ A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days).” Small AI model powerSource: Anthropic Replication experiment Anthropic ran its replication experiment using cheap Android TV boxes, and the AI models Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-26B-A4B, Llama3.1-8B, Opus 4.8, and GLM-5.2, each assigned a different role. Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.2 acted as agents tasked with setting up and propagating Llama3.1-8B (inference), while Gemma4-26B-A4B demonstrated that a model could run across 15 Android TV boxes. Opus 4.8 was separately tested as an advisor to Qwen. The experiment used a simplified setting where the targets exposed unauthenticated ADB access. Evaluation overviewSource: Anthropic The experiments showed that Qwen3.5-9B successfully installed and configured the software needed to run Llama3.1-8B on eight of the nine hardware types tested. GLM-5.2 reached all eight nodes in the controlled emulated network in four out of five trials, but the other models failed to complete the full process reliably. Anthropic observed an improvement in success rate when it retained data from previous attempts, with Qwen3.5-9 B's success rate rising from 45% early on to 84% in later generations. Improving iterationsSource: Anthropic Using the stronger Opus 4.8 model to assist Qwen in inference produced no measurable improvement. Based on the results and historical data, Anthropic predicts that models with 30 billion parameters or fewer could reach the necessary capability level by the end of 2026. On the studied hardware, the inference setup would be a slow process, taking between 28 and 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B, and 71-150 hours for Gemma4-26B-A4B, giving defenders enough time to detect and respond. However, this time could shrink with future models, so implementing stronger security measures for IoT may soon become a priority. Proposed defenses include detecting large model transfers and unusual device-to-device traffic, using honeypots to inspect payloads, quarantining infected subscribers, and improving IoT security defaults. While Anthropic’s warning is not based on an imminent threat, as their experiment failed to demonstrate full end-to-end worm-creation capability at this stage, even with lowered security settings and explicit propagation goals, the message for better IoT security remains valid. fx22yp.text: The Department of Justice disrupted multiple laptop farms across Texas allegedly being used by North Korean nationals to facilitate an IT worker scheme that allows the country to earn millions from U.S. companies. The laptop farm raids, which were conducted September 21-25, targeted more than 40 residences, the DOJ said. Law enforcement seized 187 laptops and other devices used by North Koreans. Such schemes have earned millions over the last eight years by tricking U.S. companies into hiring workers remotely into lucrative IT roles through stolen or purchased identities. Alongside the raids, the DOJ indicted and arrested U.S. nationals Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas. Several Chinese and North Korean nationals also were indicted. The department did not respond to requests for comment about whether the indictments and arrests were linked to the Texas laptop farm raids. The DOJ indicted Bostelle and Pena on wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft charges, accusing them of being key U.S.-based cogs in the IT worker scheme. Bostelle and Pena helped a group of North Koreans earn more than $3 million from about 70 U.S. companies across 17 states, prosecutors said, including organizations in healthcare, cybersecurity, retail and manufacturing. Large parts of the indictment are centered around U.S. national Trey Michael Nolte, who was not charged. The DOJ did not explain why he was not charged, but prosecutors said he ran a shell company that facilitated the scheme. Nolte allegedly communicated with Chinese and North Korean nationals, recruited Bostelle, sent packages to China, received work laptops from U.S. companies and laundered the paychecks earned by the IT workers back to North Korea. From 2019 to 2026, Bostelle and Pena hosted laptops as part of the scheme while also helping IT workers obtain and use fake identification documents to obtain employment or verify bank accounts, prosecutors said “North Korea’s rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg. “These schemes threaten the security of the IT systems and data of the deceived U.S. employers and leave countless victims of identity theft.” The actions outlined on Tuesday are part of a long-running operation to disrupt laptop farms across the U.S. as well as identify American co-conspirators who sell their identities for use or host laptop farms at their properties. Nearly 30 laptop farms across 16 states were raided last year by U.S. law enforcement. Several Americans have already been convicted and sentenced to years in prison for running laptop farms and coordinating with North Koreans on the IT worker scheme. North Korean nationals funnel the money earned from high-paying IT roles into the country’s government. Researchers have said several government agencies effectively fund themselves by employing their own coterie of IT workers. Many IT workers are located in China or Russia but a recent United Nations report found hundreds of North Korean IT workers in Laos, Cambodia and several other countries. Changing tactics Assistant FBI Director Brett Leatherman said North Korea “continues to deploy remote IT workers using stolen identities to infiltrate American companies and generate revenue for the regime and its weapons programs.” Leatherman noted that the FBI released a new public service announcement describing the latest tactics used by North Korean IT workers to recruit Americans and perpetrate the scheme. The report notes that North Korea is now taking significant steps to counter efforts by U.S. companies to stop the scheme. The scam operations are now subcontracting entire jobs to third-parties in South Asia or West Africa and hiring facilitators to conduct a wider array of tasks. “In addition to remote labor, [North Koreans] hire South Asian or West African freelancers to assist with applying to jobs and with getting hired. [They] pay these freelancers to apply manually to as many open positions as possible over a given time-period, or to conduct interviews on their behalf,” the FBI advisory said. “Increasingly, North Koreans are obtaining jobs with western companies and then hiring freelancers to complete work assignments for a fraction of the total salary. [They] subcontract employment-related remote labor to third-party freelancers, usually in Pakistan, India, Nigeria, or neighboring countries.” North Korea is also targeting low-income Americans, offering freelance gigs with mundane requests like hosting laptops or interviewing on someone’s behalf. The FBI said it has seen North Korean IT workers strategize on the best locations to connect with Americans “facing financial stress.” Those behind the scheme typically claim to be Chinese or East Asian nationals needing temporary U.S. presence or purporting to be Eastern Europeans displaced by the Russian-Ukraine war. North Koreans are “paying Americans for an expanding range of services to hide their own involvement in the scheme, including asking some to appear on camera, participate in job interviews or meetings, verify fraudulent identities, provide access to personal social media or professional networking accounts, ship packages, complete urinalysis tests or fingerprint submissions, or keep employment-related devices connected to the Internet from personal residences.” The FBI warned that when North Koreans have been caught perpetrating the scheme, they use threats of physical violence to demand payment. Others have threatened to leak sensitive corporate data if they are not paid large lump sums. “[North Koreans] have hired U.S.-based facilitators to appear in-person at victim companies or at the residences of laptop farm operators for intimidation,” the FBI said. “Facilitators paid by [North Korean IT workers] have also made in-person threats against companies that removed ITW-related accounts.” The advisory added that North Koreans are seeking to use identities that would allow them to apply for jobs that require U.S. government security clearances. IT workers “target active-duty U.S. military members to host laptops,” the FBI said. At least one active duty member of the U.S. Army has already been convicted and sentenced for allowing his identity to be used by North Korean IT workers. 1e5klur.text: An Ohio-based company allegedly collected at least $60 million by tricking panicked customers facing sextortion threats into buying help the firm didn’t provide, according to a Federal Trade Commission (FTC) complaint filed Tuesday. Digital Forensics Corporation (DFC), owner Dmitry Belkin and several affiliated companies are behind the scheme, which allegedly ran from February 2023 through July 2026, the FTC said. A federal court has temporarily ordered the “sextortion assistance” company from doing business until a decision is reached, the agency said. Desperate defendants receiving threats from sextortionists who said they will share naked photos or other sensitive sexual information with family members and employers have turned to DFC for help only to be manipulated into spending thousands, the FTC said in a press release. The company would lure victims into paying between $1,499 and $20,000 in exchange for so-called Phase 1 services that it claimed included stopping the attack, pinpointing the sextortionist’s location with a “tracking campaign,” providing a detailed investigative report, notifying law enforcement and sending a cease-and-desist letter, the complaint said. In reality, DFC did none of these things, according to the FTC. “Instead of communicating with the sextortionist through the victim's account, defendants routinely change the victim's account settings simply to block the sextortionist's communications,” the complaint said. “Instead of obtaining investigative information, defendants fabricate chat transcripts.” DFC also allegedly routinely reused pre-saved location coordinates — typically for Nigeria and the Philippines — to trick customers into believing they had located the sextortionist. The company used a script for sales calls, the complaint said, and would customize language to play to specific fears different victims might have. For example, victims in the military would be told they could face a dishonorable discharge while married victims were warned that a sextortionist could target their spouses and in-laws, the complaint said. “Defendants falsely portray themselves as digital forensics experts, claiming they can track and identify sextortionists, prevent the spread of explicit material and coordinate with law enforcement to bring criminals to justice,” the complaint said. DFC staffers allegedly told victims law enforcement would not assist them. The FBI has long recommended that victims ignore and block sextortionists, the complaint said, but the company’s workers would tell customers that doing so is “the last thing you want to do,” according to the complaint. Another level The company additionally peddled "Phase 2" services for victims willing to pay thousands of dollars more, the complaint said. While telling victims they only offered Phase 2 in rare cases, the complaint alleged that every customer was pressured into buying the second round of assistance, which purported to include ongoing monitoring of customer accounts, as well as the entire web, to defend against further attacks, the complaint said. Many customers complained to DFC, citing a contractual refund policy, but the company often would not honor it, the complaint said. Additionally, the firm allegedly used fake positive reviews while censoring negative reviews, according to the complaint. Upset customers would allegedly be given fake Better Business Bureau websites to complain to. The firm also allegedly told customers they would not receive partial refunds unless they removed negative reviews. It purchased positive phony reviews by “paying Uber drivers to post fabricated testimonials using staged photos,” the complaint said. The FTC said it has received hundreds of reports about DFC’s business practices. DFC did not respond to a request for comment. The firm allegedly marketed itself on search, video sharing and social media platforms to find victims, the press release said. The case will now be decided by a federal judge, the press release said. In March 2025, USA Today published an expose on DFC, making similar allegations. The USA Today report alleged DFC offered customers’ installment financing plans typically charging up to 18% interest and called customers dozens of times to collect payment. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

dhzuvb.text: Today is Microsoft's October 2026 Patch Tuesday, with security updates addressing a record-breaking 1,411 flaws, including one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.This Patch Tuesday addresses 70 "Critical" vulnerabilities, 57 of which are remote code execution, 11 are elevation of privileges, and 2 are spoofing.When BleepingComputer reports on Patch Tuesday security updates, we only count vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself.Therefore, today's total excludes 348 flaws fixed earlier this month, including vulnerabilities in Azure API Center, Azure App Service, Azure Event Grid, Azure SRE Agent, Mariner, Microsoft Bookings, Microsoft Dataverse, Microsoft Exchange Server, and Microsoft Partner Center.Microsoft announced today that Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 have reached end of support."Today, October 13, 2026, Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 have reached end of updates. The October 2026 monthly security update is the last update available for these editions," Microsoft said.Earlier this month, Microsoft also said organizations running Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise, Education, and IoT Enterprise editions should upgrade to newer versions as they will no longer receive security updates starting next month.This month's Patch Tuesday fixes one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.Microsoft classifies a zero-day flaw as publicly disclosed or actively exploited when no official fix is available.The actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities addressed during this October 2026 Patch Tuesday are:Microsoft patched an actively exploited zero-day security bypass flaw that allowed attackers to bypass the Mark of the Web security feature."Improper neutralization of special elements used in a command ('command injection') in Windows Shell allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network," warns Microsoft.No details have been shared on how attackers exploited the flaw or who disclosed it.Microsoft has fixed a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework that can be exploited to run unauthorized applications."Untrusted search path in .NET Framework allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally," explains Microsoft.Microsoft says this flaw could allow attackers to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement and run unauthorized applications."An authenticated attacker could place a specially crafted .NET assembly on an affected system and register it for loading by a protected process." Microsoft says."Successful exploitation could bypass Windows Defender Application Control restrictions and allow the attacker to execute code within the protected process. User interaction is not required."James Forshaw of Google Project Zero discovered the flaw.Microsoft fixed a denial-of-service flaw in MessagePack-CSharp."Improperly controlled sequential memory allocation in .NET allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network," explains Microsoft.Microsoft has not shared who disclosed the vulnerability.With this month's record-breaking number of vulnerabilities, Microsoft has also introduced a new method for organizations to prioritize security updates by grouping related flaws into what it calls "risk cohorts."The new approach groups similar vulnerabilities together to help organizations better understand which security flaws pose the greatest risk to their systems and should be prioritized for patching.Microsoft stressed that these groups do not necessarily indicate which flaws are the most dangerous, as the actual risk depends on whether they are being exploited in attacks, their severity, and how an organization uses the affected software.Microsoft says the new approach is still experimental and is meant to help organizations prioritize security updates, not replace its existing patching recommendations.Microsoft has published a PDF mapping the October 2026 vulnerabilities to their respective risk cohorts.Below is the complete list of resolved vulnerabilities in the October 2026 updates. Note, this report does include the flaws fixed earlier this month.To access the full description of each vulnerability and the systems it affects, you can view the full report here. jfc61a.text: Microsoft released the Windows 10 KB5126657 extended security update, which includes this month's record-breaking October 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes and a few bug fixes and changes. If you are running Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC or are enrolled in the ESU program, you can install this update like normal by going into Settings, clicking on Windows Update, and manually performing a 'Check for Updates.' Windows 10 KB5126657 updateSource: BleepingComputer After installing this update, Windows 10 will be updated to build 19045.7807, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 will be updated to build 19044.7807. What's new in Windows 10 KB5126657 Microsoft no longer releases new features for Windows 10, and the KB5126657 update mainly includes security updates and bug fixes. The update also includes fixes released as part of today's record-breaking October 2026 Patch Tuesday, which fixed a massive 1,411 vulnerabilities across Microsoft's products, including one actively exploited zero-day flaw. The complete list of fixes and changes in KB5126657 is listed below: [Time and Date] This update enables permanent Daylight Savings Time (DST) support for British Columbia and Alberta starting in November 2026. This update introduces the new time zone Manitoba Standard Time "(UTC-5:00) Manitoba". [ReFS security] This update adds auditing and optional policy controls for ReFS volumes on externally attached storage devices. Auditing is enabled by default, while enforcement controls remain disabled by default to give administrators time to evaluate and prepare for future security hardening changes. To learn more, see KB5130741. [Storage Spaces] Addresses an issue that might cause some Storage Spaces Direct virtual disks to remain offline after installing a Windows update. This issue occurs when valid tiered storage metadata is incorrectly identified as invalid during recovery, preventing affected virtual disks and dependent workloads from coming online. [File History (known issue)] Fixed: This update addresses an issue where File History might fail to back up or restore files to an external drive or network location. Affected devices might incorrectly display a "Reconnect your drive" message even when a compatible backup drive is connected and working properly. [Secure Boot] This update continues the deployment of updated Secure Boot certificates using the latest high-confidence targeting data to identify eligible devices that are ready to automatically receive the new certificates. Deployment through Windows Update remains ongoing across supported device. Microsoft says the update has a known issue affecting some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices after installing the September 2026 Windows security updates. Affected devices may fail to start with a Code 10 error in Device Manager, stop producing audio, or experience unresponsive volume controls and sound settings. Some devices may also work in standard stereo mode but fail when using 8-channel or 3D audio configurations. Microsoft partially fixed the issue in an emergency out-of-band update released on September 14, which addressed problems with 8-channel and 3D audio modes. However, other audio issues remain unresolved, and Microsoft says it is working on additional fixes. ze8asb.text: Microsoft announced today that devices running Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions have reached the end of support and will no longer receive monthly security and non-security preview updates. However, according to Microsoft's lifecycle policy, Windows 11 24H2 Enterprise and Education editions remain under mainstream support until October 12, 2027. "Today, October 13, 2026, Windows 11, version 24H2 Home and Pro, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016 have reached end of updates. The October 2026 monthly security update is the last update available for these editions," Microsoft said in a message center update. "Devices running these editions will no longer receive monthly security and non-security preview updates containing protections from the latest security threats." Microsoft advises users to upgrade to Windows 11 26H2, the latest Windows 11 version, also known as the Windows 11 2026 Update, which is now rolling out in phases to eligible Windows 11 devices where the "Get the latest updates as soon as they're available" option has been enabled. Windows 11 26H2 became generally available in September 2026 as an enablement package and will reach end of support for consumers in October 2029. "Windows 11, version 26H2 rollout is phased and will expand over the next few months," it added. "If the update is ready for your device, it will download and install automatically, and a single restart will complete the process." Last week, Microsoft also reminded customers that systems running Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise, Education, and IoT Enterprise editions will also stop receiving security updates in 30 days, after Windows 11 23H2 Home and Pro editions reach end of support in November 2025. Earlier this year, it extended the free Windows 10 Extended Security Updates (ESU) program for home users and announced that Windows Server 2022 also reaches the end of mainstream support today (but will remain under extended support until October 2031). More recently, on Thursday, it warned customers to upgrade devices running unsupported versions of Windows as they will stop receiving security updates after next year's Windows Update certificate rotation. More information about Windows 11 servicing dates is available on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or using the Lifecycle Policy search tool. s4sxcm.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 13, 2026Artificial Intelligence / IoT Security Small artificial intelligence (AI) models may be months away from developing capabilities to self-replicate on IoT devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes, according to a warning from Anthropic. The frontier AI lab said small AI models could form autonomous, self-propagating worm botnets that are "challenging to shut down," since "there's no centralized point to shut off." Prior work has demonstrated that AI agents can act like one by scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster with an aim to generate tailored attack strategies and use compromised machines as a botnet to run large language models (LLMs) in order to sustain its reasoning and expand in scale. "Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload." The idea, at a high level, explains how AI models could potentially break into internet-connected devices and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without having to rely on expensive data centers all the time. A more powerful model that's too large to fit into a single device could be split into small chunks and run across multiple machines to collectively run it. A threat actor could build a distributed LLM botnet from poorly secured IoT devices, making it powerful enough to run a capable model. Some of the ways an AI worm could propagate include - Small models that replicate through a compromise of host machines on which they run, also called weight-based replicators. IoT devices make for a lucrative target because of their minimal security controls. Target datacenters and other high-compute targets to set up unmonitored rogue deployments, also classified as frontier replicators or open-weight replicators based on the model used. Steal an AI service provider's API keys or platform credentials to run copies of itself, also called API-based replicators. In this case, the provider could be deceived into thinking it is serving ordinary API requests from a legitimate customer, without realizing that a malicious or self-replicating system is behind them. However, they are also likely to detect more as unusual API usage could trigger security alerts, leading to the credentials being revoked or the accounts getting blocked. A fleet of 15 Smart TV boxes running distributed inference of Gemma4-26B-A4B. In its test of 11 open-weights models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, Google, Meta MoonShot AI, OpenAI, and Zhipu AI (aka Z.ai), Anthropic said it found GLM-5.2 to be the only model to propagate Llama3.1-8B reliably to 8/8 nodes running the redroid Android emulator in 4 out of 5 trials. It also revealed that an AI IoT worm powered by inexpensive Android TV boxes could be a "slow, distributed" system that can produce a meaningful amount of AI computation when a fleet comprising hundreds of thousands of such devices is networked together to run an inference engine. Alternatively, it could take the form of a potent cyber model capable of breaching data centers at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits. "We don't yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves)," Anthropic said. "We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this."

v7n7sk.text: The U.K. Housing Ombudsman Service is investigating a third-party IT security incident that impacted its case management system on Tuesday. Established under the Housing Act 1996, the Housing Ombudsman is an executive non-departmental public body sponsored by the Ministry of Housing, Communities, and Local Government. The watchdog settles disputes between social housing residents and social landlords in England, including housing associations, landlords, managers, and letting agents. On Tuesday, the service added an alert to its official website, warning that it's working with the affected service provider to assess the incident's impact and said social housing residents cannot file new complaints until systems are back online. Those who must raise new complaints are advised to call the Housing Ombudsman's phone line or email the watchdog at info@housing-ombudsman.org.uk. "The incident has been contained, and we are working with our external supplier to establish the full facts, including the extent of the data involved," the service said. "We are continuing to investigate whether any personal information has been affected and will provide further updates as soon as we are able. " Housing Ombudsman Service alert (BleepingComputer) The Housing Ombudsman service has also notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) of the incident and advised tenants and leaseholders to be wary of potential scams when receiving unsolicited messages. "As a precaution, we recommend that individuals continue to exercise their usual caution when responding to unexpected communications," it added. "Do not disclose personal information unless you are confident of the identity of the requester and report any suspicious activity to the relevant organisation or authorities. " The watchdog is working to restore its services "as quickly as possible" and will share further updates on the investigation as soon as they're available. In March, the British government agency Companies House, which operates the registry for all U.K. companies, was also forced to take its WebFiling service offline to fix a security flaw that had exposed companies' information since October 2025. Two months earlier, in January, the United Kingdom announced a new cybersecurity strategy, backed by more than £210 million ($283 million) and aiming to boost cyber defenses across government departments and the wider public sector. 18566wt.text: A flaw in Docker Hub, the registry where container images are published and downloaded, let one user push, pull, or delete images as another user. Docker fixed the flaw on September 30 and says it found no evidence that anyone exploited it. The flaw was in the feature that converts a personal account into an organization, Docker said in a security advisory on October 12. Conversion transferred the account's personal access tokens (PATs) to the user designated as the organization's owner. A PAT is used in place of a password in the registry, and the person who created each token can still use it. The access was limited to the registry. It did not reach the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change a password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over an account. Docker tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-105445 and rated it critical. The CVE record it published on October 13 gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.4. The flaw was open from August 26, 2024, until the fix, a little over two years. Docker made the fix on Docker Hub itself, so there is no update to install. Docker Hub cannot move a repository from one account to another. A user instead converts a personal account into an organization that keeps the same name, and must name an existing account as its owner. Each personal access token acts as the account that owns it, at a permission level chosen when the token is created. While the flaw was open, conversion changed the owner recorded for each token and left its secret unchanged. An attacker could abuse this by creating a token on an account they controlled, converting that account into an organization, and naming another user as its owner. The token would then work at the registry as that user. The named owner was not asked to confirm the change and was not notified, according to Docker and the researchers who reported the flaw. Docker's conversion page has included the sentence "The new owner receives a notification email" since at least August 2024. Within the token's permission level, a transferred token could pull, push, or delete images in the named owner's repositories and in organizations the owner could access. Docker rated the flaw critical because that access "includes publishing images under a legitimate name," it said. In March and April, attackers used stolen publisher credentials to push malicious Trivy images and malicious KICS images to the publishers' own Docker Hub repositories, according to Docker. Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com found the flaw and reported it to Docker, which says it deployed the fix less than four hours after receiving their report. They named the flaw GhostPat. In their technical write-up, the two say they reproduced the flaw twice on consenting test accounts. They logged in to the registry as the target account, created and pushed to a repository in its namespace, pushed to an organization it belonged to, and pulled its private repositories. What Docker's Review Covered Docker reviewed every account conversion made while the flaw was open and compared them with registry logs and token records. It looked for any token used under more than one identity and examined every push made with a transferred token, about 304,000 in all. "We found no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited," the company said. Every one of those pushes went to a repository belonging to the converted organization or to its named owner, according to Docker. In the large majority of cases, both accounts belonged to the same person or team. Where it could not confirm that one person controlled both accounts, Docker analyzed the highest-risk public images without running them and found no malware or tampering. Docker's registry logs show when a token is used, not that it exists, so a transferred token that was never used left no record in the logs. For that reason, Docker treated every token transferred by a conversion while the flaw was open as possibly affected, whether or not it had been used. The advisory reports results for pushes. It does not say what Docker found for pulls or deletions made with transferred tokens, including pulls from private repositories. Who Was Notified and What to Check On October 2, Docker emailed the users whose accounts had received transferred tokens and, separately, the owners of the organizations involved. Each email listed the tokens by description and creation date. The advisory does not say how many users or tokens that covers, calling the group only a "limited number" of users. Anyone who did not receive the email was not exposed and has nothing to do, according to Docker. On October 8, Docker deactivated the transferred tokens it had identified. Tokens that their owners had asked to keep were not deactivated. Todd Matens, who publishes a Docker Compose linter called compose-lint, wrote in a blog post that he received two emails on October 2. One was sent to him as an organization owner and the other to his user account. He rotated his two CI tokens and checked the signatures on his 42 published images, tracing each to the CI run that built it. Docker advises users to review their tokens, revoke any they do not recognize or no longer use, and use organization access tokens, not one person's PAT, for automation that belongs to an organization. These details help with those checks: Open Account settings, then Personal access tokens. The list shows when each token was created and when it was last used. The researchers describe two traces. One is a token you did not create, whatever its name, because whoever creates a token chooses its description. The other is an organization in the account switcher that you do not remember joining. Organization access tokens require a Docker Team or Docker Business subscription. They are managed by an organization owner, a company owner, or a custom role with that permission, and they do not work with Docker Desktop or Image Access Management. Organization owners on those subscriptions can review past pushes in the activity logs, which record pushed tags and can show the token that pushed them. Docker Home, where the logs are viewed, keeps them for 30 days, and older entries are available through the Docker Hub API. Docker's Documentation Described the Transfer Docker's own documentation described the token transfer for about 17 of the roughly 25 months the flaw was open. A documentation change on April 22, 2025, added a note to Docker's conversion page. It said that naming a user as organization owner "will ensure any PATs associated with the user's account are transferred to the organization owner." Docker removed the note on September 30, minutes after the time it gives for the fix. The dates come from the public history of Docker's documentation, which The Hacker News reviewed. Docker says it now requires consent before a user is named an organization owner and notifies that user when this happens. It also records every change in token ownership and reviews other features that change who owns a credential.

1xx0f0g.text: Microsoft has released the Patch Tuesday Windows 11 KB5127648 and KB5126653 cumulative updates for versions 26H2/25H2/24H2 and 23H2 to fix security vulnerabilities and bugs, and add new features. Today's updates are mandatory as they contain the October 2026 Patch Tuesday security patches for hundreds of vulnerabilities discovered in previous months. You can install today's update by going to Start > Settings > Windows Update and clicking on 'Check for Updates.' You can also manually download and install the update from the Microsoft Update Catalog. This is the tenth 'Patch Tuesday' release in 2026, and it's based on 24H2, which means 25H2 or 26H2 get the same update. There are no exclusive or special changes. You'll get the same fixes across the two versions of Windows 11. What's new in the October 2026 Patch Tuesday update With today's update, Microsoft is adding new emojis to Windows 11 and fixing minor issues with File Explorer. Here's the full list of improvements and fixes: [File Explorer] New! This update adjusts how the preview pane handles files downloaded from the web. For HTML files, a new Preview anyway button lets you acknowledge the warning and preview the file. Non-HTML files, such as PDFs, are now previewed automatically. New! File Explorer Home now preserves the state of sections (expanded or collapsed), so you can pick up where you left off. New! This update improves the reliability of thumbnail previews for cloud files in the Details pane. The pane has also been reorganized so file properties are easier to find and review at a glance. New! The update addresses an issue that could clear the address bar contents when entering edit mode by clicking near the right side of the address bar. [Emoji] New! This update adds support for Emoji 17.0, including new emoji such as distorted face, fight cloud, and hairy creature. To insert them, press Windows + . to open the emoji panel. New! This update also refines the design of several existing emoji for better consistency across platforms, including saluting face, face with peeking eye, goose, lotus, and kissing cat. [Widgets] New! This update introduces the Tips widget, which provides short, helpful guidance about Windows features. To add it to your Widgets board, open the board, select Add widgets, and then choose Tips. To add it to your lock screen, go to Settings > Personalization > Lock screen and add Tips to your lock screen widgets. [Personalization] This update includes a variety of improvements to desktop background experiences. This update improves the reliability of the Personalization > Background page in Settings. This update adds support for using DIB image files as desktop backgrounds. This update improves reliability of desktop slideshow transitions on newly created accounts. This update improves resolution of previews when selecting a desktop background in Personalization > Background. This update improves desktop background preview display in Settings for users with portrait mode monitors. This update improves reliability of processing desktop wallpaper changes when they happen in quick succession. This update adds support for using slideshow wallpapers with multiple desktops, so that it won’t automatically switch you back to Picture. [Bluetooth] This update contains several enhancements to improve reliability and experience when connecting to and using Bluetooth devices: During voice calls, the Windows shell volume flyout now appears when adjusting the volume of a Bluetooth Classic Audio accessory via the volume controls on the accessory, providing visual feedback of the new volume level. This update improves the accuracy of the connection state displayed by Windows for accessories that have disconnected from the PC. This update improves stability of the Bluetooth and devices page in Settings when managing Bluetooth and audio devices. This update resolves an issue where the Bluetooth radio could be turned off, but the state of the radio control toggle in the Bluetooth and devices page in Settings shows as on. This update improves Bluetooth audio stability and compatibility: This update improves microphone compatibility with certain Bluetooth Classic audio accessories. This update resolves an issue that could result in a crash (error code 0x139) while streaming Bluetooth audio. This update improves reliability and performance with LE Audio accessories. This update improves the reliability of shared audio. [Accessibility] New! This update introduces Open apps maximized, an accessibility setting that automatically maximizes app windows as they open. It removes a bit of everyday friction whether you use a screen reader or magnification, work in tablet mode, or simply prefer a consistent, full-screen workspace. To turn it on, go to Settings > Accessibility > Visual effects and turn on Open apps maximized. This update improves navigation of the Bluetooth quick settings page when using keyboard input, gamepad input, or Narrator. [Magnifier] New! This update brings a modernized visual refresh to the Magnifier taskbar. Updated icons Magnifier's toolbar icons align with Windows 11 visual design, giving the tool a cleaner, more modernized feel. Refined spacing and padding The padding is adjusted with spacing across the toolbar for a more polished, consistent layout. Views, zoom controls, keyboard shortcuts, and Read Aloud all behave exactly as they did in earlier versions. [Settings] This update improves the reliability of Settings when interacting with the contents of the Settings > Bluetooth & Devices > Printers & Scanners page. This update updates Settings > Apps > Installed apps to show the version number at the top level for packaged apps, as it already does for other apps. This update improves the time picker control in Settings so that it reflects your preferred time format when you switch between 12-hour and 24-hour time. This applies in places such as setting active hours and scheduling Night light. This update improves persistence of the Allow multiple apps to use camera at the same time option in Settings > Bluetooth & Devices > Camera settings. [Touchpad] New! Additional gesture controls for precision touchpads are available in Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Touchpad: Single-finger scrolling — Scroll vertically with one finger starting from the left or right side of the touchpad. Automatic scrolling — Keep scrolling without lifting your fingers by moving them near the edge of your touchpad while scrolling. Previously, gesture controls for scroll and zoom speed and accelerate scrolling were released in the July 2026 update (KB5101684). [Copilot key] New! This update introduces a new Windows 11 setting that lets you remap the Copilot key to function as the Right Ctrl or Context Menu key, helping preserve familiar keyboard shortcuts and accessibility workflows. For more information, see Understand updates to the Copilot key on Windows devices. [Camera roll]1New! This update introduces Camera roll backup in Settings, helping eligible users protect their photos with OneDrive. You can turn on the feature from the Settings Home or Accounts page and complete setup on a mobile phone using a QR code. [Fonts] New! This update adds support for the Garay and Beria Erfe scripts to the Ebrima font, the first Microsoft font to support both. Garay was encoded in Unicode 16.0 and Beria Erfe in Unicode 17.0. New! This update also refines the Adlam glyph designs in Ebrima to align with the current Unicode standard and improve consistency. [Windows Recovery (WinRE)] New! This update adds a recovery remote management plug-in for extending WinRE management capabilities for MDM providers. For more information, see Recovery Remote Management Overview. [Kiosk mode] The Windows + Tab keyboard shortcut is now disabled when using a restricted UX kiosk. The Windows + A and Windows + C keyboard shortcuts are now disabled when using single-app kiosk mode. [Windows Backup] PC-to-PC Migration is no longer available. This feature, introduced through a phased rollout, previously allowed you to transfer files and settings directly from your previous PC when setting up a new Windows PC. To back up and restore your files, settings, and other supported items when moving to a new PC, use Windows Backup. For more information, see Backup and restore with Windows Backup. [Power and battery] This update improves display and performance in certain scenarios where a plugged-in laptop incorrectly detects a transition from AC power to battery power. Microsoft is not aware of any new issues with this month's Patch Tuesday, but it warns that some PCs might still have audio issues after the update. The bug affects USB 1.0 audio devices and isn't widespread. 18m1362.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 13, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security An attacker chained three zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure, a VPN appliance, to run commands as root without logging in, security firm Volexity said on October 13. Ivanti has released fixes for two of the flaws and told customers on affected versions to "act immediately." A fix for the third is still pending, according to Volexity. Volexity, which reported the flaws to Ivanti, found the attack on one customer's appliance. The appliance was fully patched at the time and running version 22.8R2.4. The attacker, which Volexity tracks as UTA0576, began exploiting it on October 3. Ivanti said on October 13 that it is aware of "limited exploitation in the wild." The first two flaws are an authentication bypass and a remote code execution flaw, tracked together as CVE-2026-104935. Together they let an attacker run code as the appliance's cgi-server user, and the third flaw, a privilege escalation, raises that to root, Volexity said. The CVE record Ivanti filed shows which Connect Secure versions are affected: Affected: Connect Secure "before version 25.1.3.0" Not affected: version 22.7R2.14 "or prior" Listed as unaffected: versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1 Ivanti's security advisory has more on the affected versions and the fixes. The release notes for 25.1.3.0 are dated July 2026. Customers already on that version are outside the range the CVE record gives. Ivanti is working on a fix for the privilege escalation flaw, which will come "in a future release in the coming weeks," Volexity said. Its report does not say what risk that flaw carries on an appliance where the first two are fixed. Ivanti tells customers to upgrade and to run its Integrity Checker Tool regularly. That tool misses this chain, Volexity said, because the exploit changes library code only in memory and restores the configuration data it alters. The attacker also took steps to stay hidden from the tool. Confirming a compromise takes forensic investigation, including network and memory forensics, according to Volexity. These signs come from the one incident it investigated: URL path: /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi, requested in large numbers HTTP header: X-DSCGI-PATH on those requests, with a value that does not match the URL path Directory: /data/.icscap/ IP: 108.165.147[.]64, the host the attacker used In that incident, the attacker stole stored credentials, including LDAP domain credentials, searched Active Directory for passwords, and ran password-spraying attacks against its accounts. No backdoor or web shell was left behind. The attacker reran the entire exploit chain for each command. Volexity's report and Ivanti's post do not name a temporary workaround for customers who cannot upgrade yet. They also do not say whether upgrading removes access an attacker has already gained. Volexity assessed with low confidence that UTA0576's motive is criminal, not espionage. Neither company said how many customers were attacked. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-104935 8.6 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale. In its own entry in the CVE record, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) marks exploitation as "active" and the technical impact as "total." Separately, the same Ivanti post covers fixes for two other products, Xtraction and Neurons Patch for Intune, and Ivanti said it is not aware of those flaws being exploited. Each has a flaw Ivanti rates 9.9 out of 10: CVE-2026-106042 in Xtraction before version 2026.4, and CVE-2026-109412 in Neurons Patch for Intune.

qcgox7.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 13, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security A flaw in SAP's Cloud SDK for Python can send an application's OAuth2 client credentials to a server an attacker controls, SAP said in a security advisory on October 13. The flaw affects multi-tenant applications on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) that use the SDK, SAP's official Python client for BTP services. An attacker must be able to control the tenant subdomain, the name such an application passes to the SDK to say which tenant a request is for. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-89111 and carries SAP's CVSS score of 10.0 out of 10. The advisory names version 0.45.2, released on August 21, as the fix. The SDK handles authentication for those services with the application's client credentials, a client ID and a client secret. Version 0.45.2 added a check that rejects any tenant subdomain that is not a simple name. Six later releases do not apply that check in every case, The Hacker News found. Versions 0.53.0 through 0.55.0, published between September 10 and September 18, skip it when an application calls the SDK's Destination service module. Version 0.53.0 moved that module onto new shared code for requesting tokens, and that code did not include the check. Version 0.55.1 added it there on September 18. Passing a tenant subdomain that contains URL delimiters "now raises ValueError immediately instead of silently routing credentials to an attacker-controlled endpoint," the 0.55.1 release notes say. The Hacker News ran SAP's own tests for the check on October 13, against the source code of every release from 0.45.1 to 0.58.4 and of the three 0.36 releases. The six releases failed 9 of the 11 tests SAP added with version 0.55.1. That version and the 11 releases after it passed all 11. As of October 13, the advisory lists no version above 0.45.2 as affected. Neither it nor the release notes say whether the six releases fall under CVE-2026-89111. Two releases on the older 0.36 line also lack the check. Versions 0.36.1 and 0.36.2 were published on September 4 and September 10, after the August fix, and failed the tests SAP wrote for it. Both fall inside the advisory's range of versions below 0.45.2. Releases Tenant subdomain check Basis Below 0.45.2, including 0.36.1 and 0.36.2 Missing SAP advisory. The Hacker News test of 0.36.0, 0.36.1, 0.36.2 and 0.45.1. 0.45.2 to 0.52.2 Present The Hacker News test of all 18 releases. 0.53.0 to 0.55.0 Missing for Destination calls. Also missing for Document Management Service calls in 0.55.0. SAP's 0.55.1 release notes. The Hacker News test of all 6 releases. 0.55.1 to 0.58.4 Present The Hacker News test of all 12 releases. What to Do Versions 0.45.2 through 0.52.2 and 0.55.1 through 0.58.4 contain the check. Version 0.58.4 was the newest release on PyPI, the Python package index, on October 13. Upgrading within the 0.36 line does not add the check. None of its three releases contains it. Applications that cannot upgrade yet can compare each tenant subdomain with a list of their registered tenants before passing it to the SDK, SAP says in the advisory. The flaw matters only where an application passes a tenant subdomain to the SDK. The August fix covered three modules: Agent Gateway, Destination and Document Management Service. The advisory does not say whether applications that ran a release without the check should replace their client credentials. How the Flaw Works When an application passes a tenant subdomain, the SDK requests an access token for that tenant. To do that, it takes the token URL from the application's configuration and replaces part of it with the tenant subdomain. Releases without the check used whatever value they were given. The SDK then sent the application's client ID and client secret to the resulting URL to request the token. An attacker who controls the tenant subdomain can point that request at their own server, according to SAP. The check accepts only a single name made of letters, digits and hyphens, up to 63 characters long. Any other value stops the request with an error. SAP labels the flaw server-side request forgery (SSRF), a weakness in which a server can be made to send a request to a destination it did not intend. What an attacker could do with the credentials depends on what the application's client is allowed to do. The advisory does not say. Fixed in August, Disclosed in October The unchecked code was in the SDK from its first release on PyPI, on March 16. The August release notes list the fix under "Bug Fixes" and do not mention security. "Previously, invalid values were silently used to construct a malformed URL," the notes say. The advisory followed 53 days later. It credits a GitHub user named SunandM with reporting the flaw and does not report any attacks.

152wh9p.text: TFG London detected a cybersecurity incident that impacted IT systems used by the Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles premium fashion brands. The company disclosed earlier today that several IT systems remain unavailable, although physical stores remain open for customers. According to the press release, the incident has not affected the group’s other brands, Inside Story and White Stuff, or its operations in Australia and Africa. TFG London is the UK subsidiary of South Africa’s The Foschini Group, which owns the aforementioned five fashion and homeware brands. As of mid-2026, the group operated 649 retail locations globally and reported annual sales of £488 million ($646M). The company said it detected the cyberattack on October 11 and immediately activated its incident response and business continuity plans, bringing in external cybersecurity experts to help contain the threat. TFG London is investigating whether any customer information has been compromised, and says it will notify affected individuals or organizations if it data has been affected. BleepingComputer could not find any threat actor publicly claiming the TFG London breach. The incident at TFG London comes shortly after another UK fashion retailer, ASOS, suffered a data breach after hackers sent push notifications to users of its mobile app. The company later confirmed that attackers used social engineering to steal an employee’s login credentials and gained unauthorized access to customer data, including names, contact details, and account information. At this time, TFG London has not confirmed any customer data exposure, but clients of Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles are advised to remain alert for potential phishing and social engineering attacks. Earlier this week, rumors emerged about an attack at Swedish multinational clothing company H&M, claimed by an attacker saying they were with the ShinyHunters group and threatening to leak stolen data. Responding to our request for a comment on these allegations, an H&M spokesperson said they were looking into these claims, although current evidence didn't indicate a breach. “We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims,” the H&M spokesperson told BleepingComputer. “At this time, we have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised.” Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.
