1735tqr.text: GitHub has taken the step of expiring unvalidated npm trusted publishing configurations 48 hours after creation after researchers found that it was possible for an attacker to push new versions of a different user's package without having to steal their credentials. "Your configuration becomes validated and exempt from expiry after its first successful publish," the Microsoft-owned subsidiary said. "Changing the repository or project identity requires a new trust relationship with a fresh 48-hour validation window -- ordinary edits don't restart the deadline." The change contains the risk associated with trusting a repository or project name that changes ownership, GitHub said, adding npm also rejects trusted publishing tokens from GitHub Actions issue_comment events going forward, along with the Existing pull_request_target restriction. In an update to its documentation, GitHub states that a newly created trusted publisher configuration must complete its first successful publish within two days, which validates the configuration and binds it to the "repository's immutable identity." The development comes in response to findings from Bloom Security, which discovered a loophole within npm's trusted publishing to take over thousands of packages and trigger a Shai-Hulud-style cascading supply chain attack. The findings were reported to GitHub on June 6, 2026. "Imagine this: an attacker compromises a single package. An AI agent on a popular package maintainer's device autonomously pulls it for a project," security researcher Golan Myers said. "That single endpoint is used to push malicious code to the popular package. All the package users are exposed. All because one person with the correct access was exposed." Trusted publishing was introduced in npm in July 2025 as a credential-free authentication method that allows developers to push npm packages from a CI/CD platform, such as GitHub Actions, using OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens. When trusted publishing is configured, the developer's CI/CD provider generates a short-lived cryptographic token for a specific workflow run that the npm registry verifies against a pre-authorized configuration. This eliminates the need to store, rotate, or manually manage long-lived npm secrets, reducing the risk of credential leaks. It also automatically generates provenance attestations for npm packages, allowing users to establish where a package was built and who published it, thereby strengthening software supply chain security. However, as Bloom Security found, this security architecture suffered from a problem in how it identified that repository, also called a slug (i.e, the combination of the owner or organization and the repository name that's formatted as "owner/repository"). "It records the repository's address, [...] instead of the permanent ID GitHub assigns it, at least until a version is first published from that repository," Myers explained. "It is like a lock that checks the address on the door rather than who owns the house: when the owner moves out, whoever moves in gets the key." Put differently, the numeric IDs that survive through repository renaming and transfers are carried by GitHub's OIDC tokens, but are completely ignored by npm until the first successful publish from that repository. This means the trust is anchored to a name as opposed to an immutable repository ID, a loophole that can be abused by claiming abandoned slugs to inherit their trust. For this attack to succeed, the only prerequisite is that the victim's trusted publisher points to a GitHub slug an attacker can claim, and the repository has never been used to publish a version of the package to npm. Once such a slug becomes available for use after a maintainer renames, transfers, or deletes a repository, an attacker can follow the steps below - Create a repository at the freed slug at the "owner/repository" path, which causes GitHub to issue a fresh repository ID. Create and trigger an npm publish workflow, which mints an OIDC token carrying the reclaimed slug and the new numeric repository ID Submit the token to the npm exchange endpoint. Npm finds that the repository claim matches the stored slug and issues a publish credential. The attacker receives a time-limited publish token for a package they do not own and pushes malicious changes to the registry. An attack of this kind, codenamed SlugFest, can be abused to publish a new "malicious" version of the victim package under the legitimate package name, while inheriting existing reputation, download counts, and dependent relationships. This, in turn, can lead to supply chain attacks at scale. AI agents running on developer machines can further complicate matters. "Agents resolve dependencies on their own, tend to take the latest version, and rarely check where a package came from," Bloom Security said. "A malicious version published through a reclaimed slug gets pulled in and runs with no human-in-the-loop." The cybersecurity company said it found over 1,500 vulnerable packages that have been collectively downloaded more than 10 million times. Developers who maintain npm packages are advised to perform the following actions - Audit trusted publisher bindings and verify if the listed repository slug still resolves to the repository under their control. If the repository has been renamed or transferred, delete the existing trust binding and re-create it pointing at the current slug. Monitor for unexpected npm publish events. Delete trust bindings every time a repository is deleted, transferred, or renamed. "The attack requires no insider knowledge, no credential theft, and no race condition," Myers said. "The only precondition is slug availability (on a binding that has not yet been used to publish), which is entirely a function of the victim's own repository hygiene." "What this research demonstrates is something the security community has seen repeatedly across supply chain attacks: the binding between a human-readable identifier and the thing it identifies is the most important invariant in any trust system. When that binding can be silently replaced – by the ordinary act of renaming a repository, not by any attacker action – the trust guarantee collapses." This is not the first time unconventional supply chain attack vectors have been discovered. Earlier this August, Bloom Security also found that both Open VSX and Microsoft's VS Code Marketplace allowed extension packs to reference non-existent extensions in the marketplaces. The technique, referred to as Extension Resurrection, can be weaponized to hijack extensions already referenced inside these trusted bundles just by claiming a namespace left unclaimed. As many as 87 packs in Open VSX and 677 packs in the VS Code Marketplace were flagged as vulnerable. "Attackers could claim those empty slots, publish malicious code under them, and have it installed automatically alongside the trusted pack – silently pushing updates to anyone who installed the pack previously," Myers noted at the time. "Because extensions run with full host access, this effectively amounts to [remote code execution] delivered under the guise of legitimacy."

j7np1u.text: Cybersecurity researchers on Monday said they discovered a vulnerability in a widely used AI development sandbox that could allow rogue agents to leak sensitive information by bypassing restrictions designed to keep them isolated. The new research, published by AI security startup AIR, found that a network filtering flaw in Vercel Sandbox — a tool used to run code in isolated environments — could allow agents to exploit certificate validation processes to transmit data outside approved networks. “This vulnerability shows that enterprises can have Hugging Face [style] mini incidents with their own agents,” Niv Hoffman, AIR co-founder and CTO, told Recorded Future News in an interview. “The new contribution our research makes is [showing] that even in the standard hardened sandbox of today, there are still flaws that will make an agent going rogue manage to escape the sandbox and do things in the wild.” Developers typically use sandboxes to prevent AI agents from accessing unauthorized systems or transmitting sensitive information. Network allowlists restrict communication to approved destinations, preventing agents from connecting to untrusted servers. AIR researchers found that rogue agents could circumvent those restrictions by exploiting the way servers handle digital certificates. In a scenario demonstrated by the researchers, a specific certificate was designed that could be sent to an approved server and could then trigger a request to an attacker-controlled server, allowing the information to be transmitted without the sandbox ever directly communicating with the unauthorized destination. “A crafted certificate is all it takes,” the report said. “The wall meant to keep your secrets in has a door, and the agent holds the key.” “It’s a very hard leak to patch,” Hoffman said. “This sandbox never communicated directly with the attack server… so from the sandbox perspective, everything looked fine.” Hoffman said his team contacted Vercel about the vulnerability and the company said it needs time to find a patch because “it's unclear for them right now how it's going to be done.” Vercel did not immediately respond to a request for comment. AIR has not found evidence of any exploitation of the vulnerability in the wild, but can’t rule out whether or not there has been one, Hoffman said, underscoring that the vulnerability in the Vercel sandbox appeared to be longstanding. The research is important because it shows that an approved server can become an “unwitting courier for stolen credentials,” according to Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of 0rcus, a cyberkinetics company. “Security has to account for what happens after the first connection.” No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1xv0zuq.text: Police in Ghana and Nigeria arrested or detained 28 people and identified more than 100 suspected victims of human trafficking during an international operation targeting scam compounds in West Africa, U.S. and British officials announced Tuesday. The operation was hosted by Britain’s National Crime Agency (NCA) in London last week. It brought together 15 law enforcement agencies and the same number of tech companies — including Meta, Microsoft and Google — as part of what they called Joint Disruption Week. In Ghana, authorities raided a compound in Sasaabi, a semi-rural community outside the capital, Accra, arresting 19 people and seizing 303 devices, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. Nigerian authorities made nine further arrests. The Ghanaian police also identified 117 people whom the department described as trafficking victims and said were “rescued” and now awaiting repatriation to Nigeria, alongside 89 scam victims who had lost an estimated $8.3 million. “These networks steal savings on one side of the screen, and people’s freedom on the other,” said Matthew Floyd, a deputy assistant director in the FBI’s Criminal Division. The Department of Justice said the technology companies it worked with removed more than 3.7 million accounts, pages and groups linked to the West African scam centres. Meta’s Rob Cochrane gave the same figure for Facebook and Instagram alone. The department did not break the total down by company. “The disrupted schemes included law enforcement impersonation scams, digital ‘arrest’ extortion schemes, cryptocurrency investment fraud (also known as ‘pig butchering’), and a variety of other online fraud operations targeting global victims,” stated the DOJ. Following the police action in West Africa, officials said more than $11 million in “potentially freezable” funds had been identified, but did not say how much had been frozen or seized. The FBI’s Floyd described identifying assets as “the easy part.” Nick Sharp, the NCA’s deputy director of fraud, said it was not yet known how many British or American victims the compounds had targeted, as forensic work on seized devices continues. The Meta connection U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said the operation began with information from Meta, which the NCA also credited as playing “a key role in coordinating the event and encouraging broad private sector participation to maximize scam compound disruption.” Pirro — a former Fox News host and longtime ally of President Donald Trump — said she was “very proud to work with Meta.” She credited all of the participating businesses with having “voluntarily disrupted scam infrastructure” on their platforms, adding: “And thank God for them.” Her praise for Meta comes as the company faces scrutiny over fraud on its platforms and questions about whether the right incentives exist for the company to properly tackle such fraud. A Reuters investigation last year, citing internal company documents, reported that Meta projected about 10% of its 2024 revenue, roughly $16 billion, would come from ads linked to scams and banned goods. Meta disputes that figure and says scams undermine the trust its advertising business depends on. Last November, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, (D-CT) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) urged the Federal Trade Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether Meta profited from scam advertising and whether enforcement action was warranted. Other lawmakers have pushed for broader changes. In February, Sens. Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) and Bernie Moreno (R-OH) introduced the bipartisan SCAM Act, which would require social media companies to take “reasonable steps” to verify advertisers and combat fraudulent ads or face action from the FTC and state attorneys general. Earlier this year, Trump signed an executive order focused on cybercrime, fraud and scam centers, emphasizing law enforcement coordination, diplomacy and victim restitution rather than imposing direct new obligations on tech platforms. Asked by Recorded Future News whether Meta would require identity verification for all advertisers, Cochrane pointed to earlier targets for verifying high-risk advertisers. The company said it is aiming for verified advertisers to account for 90% of its ad revenue by the end of 2026, up from 70% today, arguing that the remaining 10% would low-risk unverified businesses such as “local ice cream shops.” No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

1mice51.text: Ivanti urged customers on Tuesday to immediately patch an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability in the Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) remote access gateway. Formerly known as Pulse Connect Secure and originally Juniper Pulse, the enterprise-grade ICS SSL VPN provides remote employees, contractors, and hybrid workforces with secure access to corporate and cloud resources. Tracked as CVE-2026-104935, this high-severity authentication bypass zero-day affects ICS versions 22.8R2.4 and earlier, 25.1.2.2 and earlier, and 25.1.1.1 and earlier. Remote threat actors without privileges can exploit CVE-2026-104935 in low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction to execute arbitrary commands on targeted ICS appliances. "At the time of disclosure, Ivanti is aware of limited exploitation in the wild. We are working directly with those organizations while making information, updates and remediation available to the broader customer community. If you are running one of the impacted versions, Ivanti recommends you act immediately," Ivanti said. "Customers should review the security advisory, upgrade to the fixed version as soon as possible, and run the Integrity Checker Tool regularly." Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 5,500 ICS instances exposed online, but there is no information on how many are honeypots or have already been secured against ongoing attacks. Internet-exposed ICS instances (Shadowserver) Exploited since at least October 3 Cybersecurity firm Volexity, which found and reported the flaw, revealed earlier today that a previously unknown threat actor it tracks as UTA0576 has chained the CVE-2026-104935 vulnerability since at least October 3 with two other flaws to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution on fully patched devices. "Notably, UTA0576 deployed no malware or web shell. Instead, the threat actor re-exploited the device for every command it ran and tampered with logs to cover its tracks, evading Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool," Volexity said. While Ivanti has patched two flaws, it is still working to address a privilege escalation vulnerability that UTA0576 exploited as part of the same chain. Threat intelligence company Defused also confirmed Volexity's report, saying that it caught the first signs of CVE-2026-104935 exploitation in the wild starting October 1. ​Hackers have frequently exploited Ivanti vulnerabilities, often as zero-days, because they provide a quick way to breach enterprise networks and steal sensitive customer and corporate data. Ivanti has also patched several other Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild over the past several years, some of them chained in widespread attacks to deploy malware. It addressed an authentication bypass (CVE-2023-46805) and a command injection (CVE-2024-21887) in early January 2024, and a server-side request forgery (CVE-2024-21893) two weeks later. More recently, it fixed a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability tracked as CVE-2025-0282 in January 2025 and a second RCE flaw (CVE-2025-22457) that China-linked cyber spies have exploited since at least mid-March 2025. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 36 vulnerabilities across various Ivanti products as actively exploited in the wild since November 2021, 12 of which ransomware gangs have also abused. Ivanti has over 3,000 employees, a network of over 7,000 partners, and more than 40,000 customers worldwide using its IT asset management solutions. 15j8hev.text: Docker has disclosed a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-105445) in Docker Hub that let attackers access another user’s container repositories using a personal access token (PAT). Docker Hub is an online registry for storing, sharing, and downloading container images - templates that package everything needed for an application to run in an isolated environment. In Docker Hub, a PAT serves as a secret used to authenticate tools and workflows. It allows you to pull, push, or delete container images. According to a security bulletin from the Docker team, an attacker could create an account and PAT, then convert the account into an organization and name a target user as its owner. The CVE-2026-105445 flaw stems from Docker Hub reassigning a personal access token (PAT) to a designated organization owner without changing its secret or obtaining the target's consent. This allowed the attacker to use the token to authenticate as the target. Depending on the token’s scope and the target’s permissions, attackers could pull, push, or delete images in the target’s repositories and accessible organizations. “Within the scope of the token, a re-assigned PAT acted as the target user at the registry level, meaning an attacker could potentially pull, push, and/or delete images in the target’s repositories and in organizations where the target had access,” Docker explained. “Because that includes publishing images under a legitimate name, we treated this as a software supply chain risk and rated it critical.” Although the flaw is critical, Docker noted that it did not provide Docker Hub web access or allow attackers to change passwords, email addresses, or two-factor settings, potentially locking legitimate account holders out. The vulnerability was introduced on August 26, 2024, when the conversion started reassigning the personal account PAT to the new owner. This occurred without revoking or rotating the secret, and without asking the named owner to confirm the change. On September 30, 2026, Docker received a vulnerability report describing the issue, confirmed it, and deployed a fix to production less than four hours later. Docker says it found no evidence of exploitation after examining 304,000 pushes made with transferred tokens and analyzing high-risk public images. Affected users and organization owners were notified on October 2, and transferred PATs were deactivated on October 8, except for those whose owners explicitly requested to retain them. Docker says users who didn’t receive a notification should assume they were not impacted and did not need to take any action. The platform no longer transfers PATs during conversion and requests user consent before naming them an organization owner. 1f59lyd.text: North Korean hackers have been targeting Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security and international policy amid Pyongyang’s growing military cooperation with Russia, according to a new report. As part of the campaign, the hacking group Kimsuky used fake conference invitations, research collaboration requests and malicious documents designed to steal information, South Korean cybersecurity firm Genians said in a report published Monday. North Korea has provided troops to fight in the war in Ukraine as well as other military support to Russia since 2024. "Kimsuky’s attacks against Ukraine may be aimed at collecting information on the war, the extent of North Korean troop losses, developments in the questioning and handling of prisoners of war, and the details of consultations between South Korea and Ukraine,” researchers said, adding that most of the observed attacks were unsuccessful. Genians said the transfer of two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces to South Korea in September could also be of intelligence interest to Pyongyang, particularly what the prisoners might disclose about North Korean military operations and casualties. Operation GitPower In one attack in August, the hackers impersonated organizers of a cybersecurity conference in Seoul and invited a Ukrainian security expert to speak at the event. The email included genuine details about the conference and offered to cover travel and accommodation expenses. It initially did not contain malicious links or attachments. Instead, the attackers encouraged the recipient to respond before sending additional materials. In another case, the hackers posed as a European policy researcher seeking feedback on a report about military cooperation between Russia and North Korea. After the recipient responded, the attackers sent a link to a malicious archive disguised as research material, according to Genians. The hackers also used files disguised as PDF documents and legitimate Zoom installers to trick recipients into running malicious software. The malware was designed to collect information from infected computers, maintain access to compromised systems and send stolen information to infrastructure controlled by the attackers. Researchers also identified Japanese-language documents on infrastructure associated with the campaign, suggesting the hackers may have been preparing attacks against Japanese-speaking targets. These attacks are part of a broader cyberespionage campaign tracked as Operation GitPower, which uses legitimate software development platforms, including GitHub, GitLab and Codeberg, to distribute malicious files and communicate with compromised systems, researchers said. Broader espionage campaign Kimsuky has been active since at least 2012, targeting governments, think tanks, academics, and media organizations across Asia, Europe, Japan, Russia and the United States. In 2023, the U.S. and its Pacific allies imposed sanctions on the group, accusing it of collecting intelligence to support North Korea’s foreign policy and sanctions-evasion efforts. In May 2025, cybersecurity firm Proofpoint reported that a North Korean-linked group tracked as TA406 had been sending malicious emails to Ukrainian government agencies, potentially seeking intelligence about the risks facing North Korean troops fighting alongside Russian forces. According to Proofpoint, TA406’s cyber operations in Ukraine focus on political intelligence and strategic analysis of the war, in contrast to Russian hackers, who typically seek tactical intelligence related to battlefield operations. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

6sg7yh.text: On August 4, 2026, an Akira ransomware affiliate began spraying passwords against a SonicWall SSL VPN. Around seven minutes later, one attempt succeeded. The credentials were valid, and the VPN account had no multi-factor authentication (MFA) protecting it. Roughly two hours later, the attacker used RDP to access the domain controller and began enumerating Active Directory. The ransomware deployment ultimately failed, but by then the attacker had already stolen credentials and file-share data. It highlights an issue that is still common in 2026, where an organization might require MFA for Microsoft 365 and other SaaS applications while leaving certain access paths protected only by passwords. It’s this gap that attackers are regularly exploiting. Stolen Credentials Remain a Valuable Tool for Attackers Once an attacker has a valid account, they can begin interacting with the environment through the same authentication mechanisms used by legitimate employees and administrators. AI is adding another dimension to this problem by helping attackers operate at greater speed and scale. The underlying identity tactics are largely unchanged: attackers still compromise identities, reuse credentials, escalate privileges and misuse legitimate access. The threat is that AI makes familiar techniques cheaper and easier to run at scale. Mandiant’s ransomware investigations illustrate why that matters once credentials are obtained. Compromised legitimate credentials accounted for initial access in 21% of the 2025 incidents where the entry point could be established, typically through RDP or VPN. RDP also appeared frequently later in the attack chain, with attackers using compromised or newly created accounts over RDP for lateral movement in around 85% of the ransomware incidents it investigated. Identifying Stolen Credentials in Your Organization Strong authentication helps limit what an attacker can do with a stolen password, but it is still worth finding exposed or risky credentials before they are used. Password reuse, weak choices and credentials that have appeared in previous breaches all increase the chance that an attacker will find a password that still works somewhere in the environment. That makes regular password auditing a useful part of Active Directory security. Specops Password Auditor is a free, read-only password auditing tool that scans Active Directory for password-related vulnerabilities and presents the findings in an interactive report covering user and password policy information. This gives IT teams another opportunity to reduce credential risk at source: identify password weaknesses, address them where possible, and make sure that a compromised password is not enough on its own to gain access. Why Cloud MFA Doesn’t Necessarily Protect the Entire Windows Estate Microsoft 365, identity providers and SaaS applications are obvious places to add additional authentication factors because they are internet-facing and frequently targeted. The problem is that cloud MFA does not automatically extend to every system that relies on the same user identity. A user may need MFA to access a SaaS application through the corporate identity provider, but the same account could still be accepted elsewhere with just a password. That creates a fragmented authentication environment where some routes are better protected than others, which leaves a gap for attackers to exploit. VPNs are another potential gap. As the August Akira ransomware attack demonstrated, a threat actor that obtains or brute forces a valid username and password may be able to turn those credentials directly into remote network access if MFA isn’t enforced. For IT and security teams, the useful question is therefore not simply whether MFA is deployed, but where a password is still enough on its own. Windows logon, RDP, VPN access and older AD-backed services are all worth including in that review. Closing the Authentication Gaps Closing these gaps means applying stronger authentication to the places where credentials are still being trusted, rather than treating MFA as something that only sits in front of cloud applications. That is where solutions like Specops Secure Access fit by extending MFA to Windows logon, RDP and VPN authentication. This adds strong protection to some of the access paths attackers regularly target with stolen Active Directory credentials. It also supports SSO for SaaS applications through OIDC and SAML, helping organizations apply a more consistent authentication approach across on-premises and cloud services. Authentication is also a useful source of security telemetry. Specops Secure Access integrates with SIEM, SOC and analytics platforms, allowing authentication events and suspicious activity to feed into the wider monitoring process. Protecting the user is only part of the picture, though. A second question is whether the device making the request should be trusted. Mitigate the Risk of Stolen Passwords In 2026, stolen passwords are still powerful tools for attackers if they are accepted by VPNs, RDP sessions or Windows systems without additional checks. That is why MFA coverage matters as much as adopting MFA in the first place. Protecting cloud applications is important, but it does not remove the risk created by authentication paths elsewhere in the environment that still rely on a password alone. No single control will stop every intrusion, and MFA is no exception. But organizations can make credential theft much less useful by asking a simple question: where can a password still be used on its own? Adding another protective layer to those areas with Specops Secure Access ensures that one stolen credential does not become the easiest route into the rest of the network. If you’re looking to close gaps in your identity security strategy, book a demo with Specops today. Sponsored and written by Specops Software.

1awidxq.text: SAP has addressed 20 security flaws across multiple products in its October 2026 security updates, including a maximum-severity vulnerability in the Cloud SDK for Python. The SAP Python SDK is the official programmatic toolkit for developing AI agents and Python applications on the company's SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) services. Tracked as CVE-2026-89111, the maximum-severity vulnerability patched this month can be exploited by remote attackers without privileges to steal credentials. Customers who can't immediately deploy the October 2026 SAP patches can temporarily mitigate the issue by using an allowlist to validate tenant_subdomain values. "The SAP Cloud SDK for Python contains an OAuth2 SSRF vulnerability affecting multi-tenant BTP applications. An attacker who controls the tenant_subdomain parameter can redirect OAuth2 token requests to an attacker-controlled server, causing client credentials to be exfiltrated," according to a Tuesday advisory. "Consumer applications can mitigate the vulnerability by validating tenant_subdomain against a known allowlist of registered tenant subdomains before passing it to any SDK call." Today, SAP also addressed CVE-2026-89110, a critical broken access control vulnerability in the SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer that could let remote attackers with limited privileges fully compromise vulnerable systems. Another critical flaw patched today in SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence (tracked as CVE-2026-89108) lets threat actors with administrator privileges gain admin control over the underlying system by provisioning an elevated-privilege account on the underlying Java app. In recent months, SAP has fixed several other maximum-severity flaws in multiple components. For instance, it patched CVE-2026-58231 in the Commerce Cloud cloud-based e-commerce platform in August, which threat intelligence firm Defused flagged as actively exploited in attacks days after it was addressed. More recently, in September, it also fixed the CVE-2026-44756 memory corruption flaw in the SAP Kernel code, dubbed OVERPASS by Onapsis security researchers who reported it. According to Onapsis estimates at the time, over 10,000 Internet-facing SAP systems use the vulnerable component and may be exposed to attacks that exploit CVE-2026-44756. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added 14 SAP security flaws to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities since November 2021, three of which were abused in ransomware attacks. SAP is a German multinational software company that serves 99 of the 100 largest companies worldwide and reported revenues exceeding €36 billion in fiscal year 2025. Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed. Save your seat

1a7w9zk.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 13, 2026Data Privacy / Compliance The Norwegian Data Protection Authority (DPA) has fined Xandr, an advertising unit owned by Microsoft, €8.6 million ($9.62 million) for illegally relaying ​Grindr users' sensitive data to advertisers. The administrative penalty is the largest issued by the data protection watchdog, arguing the case merited a high fine because of the "very serious" nature of the breach. The infringements occurred between July 2018 and April 2020. "Xandr acted as an intermediary that relayed the personal data of Grindr users in Norway, including data revealing sexual orientation, to potentially thousands of other companies," the Data Protection Authority said in a statement. The data protection authority said its investigation found that Xandr was a joint controller with Grindr, which meant it was responsible for obtaining users' consent before processing their data. Instead of ensuring they had the legal basis for their own processing of the data, Xandr pointed fingers at Grindr, stating it assumed the online dating app had collected users' consent to do so," it added. Xandr was formed by AT&T following its June 2018 acquisition of AppNexus. The name is a reference to Alexander Graham Bell, who founded AT&T in 1885. It was subsequently sold to Microsoft in late December 2021, following which the brand was retired and consolidated under the Microsoft Ads umbrella in June 2023. The case dates back to 2020, when the country's consumer council, along with Austrian privacy non-profit None of Your Business (noyb), filed a complaint against Xandr, accusing it of unlawfully sharing users' personal data for commercial purposes without getting users' explicit consent. Thousands of users in Norway are said to have been subjected to unlawful sharing of their sensitive data as a result of this practice. "The essence of the infringement was Xandr's participation in so-called real-time bidding, where they acted both on the buyer and seller side," the watchdog said. "When a person opened Grindr, their personal data was in many cases relayed through Xandr to potentially thousands of actors in the advertising ecosystem." "Advertisers could thereby bid against each other to present targeted adverts, completely hidden from the individual user." The DPA also said the fine was calculated taking into account Xandr's total annual turnover during the two-year time period, which predates Microsoft's acquisition. Xandr has three weeks to appeal the decision. Responding to the DPA's decision, noyb described the fine as a "major blow for the online advertising and commercial surveillance industry" and said that "companies such as Xandr are eventually held accountable for their shady practices." In a statement shared with Reuters, Microsoft said it's reviewing the decision and assessing its options. Last month, Grindr opted to pay £26 million ($35.1 million) to settle a lawsuit in the U.K. over allegations that it shared users' personal information, including their HIV status, with third-parties. The development comes as a Texas federal judge granted final approval of a $177 million AT&T settlement for classes of AT&T consumers whose personal information was exposed in two separate data breaches that took place in March and July 2024. The class-action lawsuit was settled in November 2025. The March 2024 incident involved the publication of a dataset on the dark web containing Social Security numbers. It affected about 7.6 million current AT&T account holders and approximately 65.4 million former account holders, the telecom service provider noted at the time. The second hack revolved around threat actors illegally downloading AT&T customer data from a third-party cloud platform hosted by Snowflake. The American company said that calls and text message records that occurred between May 1 and October 31, 2022 were compromised for "nearly all" cellular customers.

1p2653e.text: The Hacker NewsOct 13, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Identity Security The dangerous part of a stolen identity isn't always the initial login. It's what an attacker can do with that access next. With AI accelerating reconnaissance, exploitation of vulnerabilities, and privilege escalation, attackers can move through systems faster than security teams can investigate. A compromised account that looks legitimate at first could become the starting point for a much larger attack. And that's where traditional identity security faces a serious problem: Checking who gets access isn't enough if you can't control what happens after. Why Traditional Identity Controls Are Falling Behind Many identity security controls focus on authentication, permissions, and access policies. But what happens when a trusted identity is compromised, its behavior changes, or an attacker begins exploiting already granted privileges? That gap becomes more dangerous as AI-powered attacks accelerate. Attackers can automate parts of the attack chain while defenders are still collecting alerts, investigating activity, and deciding how to respond. The answer isn't simply detecting attacks faster. It's the ability to evaluate and control access in real time while an identity is actively being used. This is the idea behind runtime identity security. In this upcoming expert-led webinar, you'll learn: Where attackers find identity gaps across cloud, on-premises, SaaS, and AI environments. Why AI-powered attacks challenge traditional defenses and reduce the time available to respond. How runtime identity security works to evaluate access continuously and enforce security decisions when they matter. How to prepare your defenses for AI-driven attacks that move at machine speed. The Next Identity Attack May Not Give You Time to React If attackers can compromise identities and escalate privileges in minutes, discovering suspicious activity after the fact may already be too late. Security teams need to know not just who has access, but whether that access should still be trusted right now. This session explores how to close that gap and build an identity security strategy designed to keep pace with the speed of modern attacks. 📅 Save Your Spot: Watch the Webinar

1kpsqwl.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 13, 2026Vulnerability / IoT Security Three vulnerabilities in LG's webOS can be chained to give an attacker on the same local network root access to certain smart TVs without a PIN or any interaction from the owner. LG has issued a fix, according to an advisory published by SSD Secure Disclosure on October 12. The chain was tested on two TV models, the 32LQ636BPSA and the 27TQ600SW, running webOS 7.5.7-25 on firmware 04.54.40. Whether other models or firmware versions are affected is not known. Owners of affected TVs should check for a firmware update. No workaround is available for those who cannot update yet. The attack enters through a service that the TV exposes on port 3001, which is used by the LG ThinQ app for pairing. An attacker replays a manifest from sync-demo, a built-in app already on the device, signed with a test certificate the firmware trusts. A permission in the manifest causes the pairing service to skip the PIN prompt and hand over a privileged key. With that key, the attacker launches another built-in app, cmp-client, and points it to an attacker-controlled page. The app does not check where it navigates, and the loaded page keeps access to PalmServiceBridge, an internal interface to the TV's system services. Through that bridge, the attacker calls the system logging service, pmlogd, passing shell commands through an input field the service does not check. Because pmlogd runs as root, the injected command runs as root. This is not the first time the local network attack surface has led to root access on LG smart TVs. In 2024, Bitdefender disclosed a different set of webOS vulnerabilities that also allowed unauthenticated access from the network, affected different components, and were patched in March 2024. A separate chain demonstrated at TyphoonPWN 2025 used a path traversal on a different port. The chain was demonstrated by an anonymous researcher who won third place in the LG webOS category at TyphoonPWN 2026, held in Seoul in May. No CVE identifiers have been assigned, and no exploitation in the wild has been reported.

rj2db6.text: A user opens a browser tab, pastes data into a chat assistant, and nothing is installed. A developer adds a coding assistant as an editor extension, and nothing shows up in the installed programs list. Someone downloads a local model runtime, a program that runs models directly on the machine instead of sending data to an external service, because they were told not to send company data outside. None of this reaches your software inventory. Tasked with controlling AI, an administrator often resorts to blocking well-known AI websites and taking enforcement action without knowing what is actually running. Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control (AIVC) is the discovery and risk layer that answers the questions you have, first: Which AI software is present on your protected Windows endpoints, who is running it, and how much risk does each one carry. What Your Software Inventory Was Never Built to Watch AI Visibility and Control covers four classes of exposure, and each one sits outside a control you already own. AI services reached through the browser. Hosted assistants are the path most organizations already worry about. The inventory identifies which services are running, on which machines, and whether you have marked them as approved. A service with no findings is not automatically approved; a clean result on a tool your organization never sanctioned is still shadow AI. This ensures filtering decisions are based on real user activity rather than hand-picked domain lists.AI inside the development environment. Coding assistants run inside editors that already hold source repositories, and often credentials and configuration files in the same working directory. They are rarely covered by whatever you decided about chat assistants, because nobody classified them as the same kind of tool.AI running locally on the endpoint. Local model runtimes, MCP servers, and agent frameworks execute on the machine itself. A control that governs which websites an endpoint may reach does not see them at all. The MCP server is the sharpest case: its entire purpose is to hand a model access to something else, and it usually arrives as a configuration entry rather than as an install.AI with reach into other systems. Where a tool is configured to connect to a database, a code repository, an internal API, or a third-party model service, that connection is part of your attack surface. AI Visibility and Control records the configured scope of those connections, not the data moving across them. How AIVC Finds and Categorizes What It Finds GravityZone AI Visibility and Control discovery takes place during the risk scan. The GravityZone BEST agent collects metadata from each endpoint and keeps that collection minimized: it records what AI software is present and how it is configured, not what anyone does with it. AIVC does not inspect prompts, chat history, model weights, credentials, or full file content. AI Visibility and Control recognizes more than 50 AI agents and more than 70,000 skills, the modular code packages that extend an agent's capabilities and that arrive from public registries. Because agents exercise permissions through these skills, considering only agents while ignoring skills would account for only a fraction of the total exposure. Every discovered service is assigned to one of 17 functional categories based on its primary function (e.g., LLMs, coding, productivity, and others). The category makes the inventory actionable at the policy level because it maps to the question the reviewer arrived with. A security team investigating data-handling risk, filters to LLMs and chatbots plus Platforms and infrastructure. A development manager auditing what touches source code goes straight to Coding and Tools and skills. A governance review covering automation risk works from Agents, Automation, and MCP. Two Views, and a Connector Nobody Installed AI Visibility and Control appears in Bitdefender GravityZone Console as two views, each answering a different question. AI Services answers "what AI is running in my environment?" It is the inventory: every discovered service with its risk score. This includes the function category, the related AI assets it depends on or exposes, its count of open findings, the affected resources and endpoints it was found on, its state of Active or Ignored, and whether it sits on the watchlist. Opening a service shows its details alongside mitigation guidance. AI Findings answers "what should I look at first?" It is the prioritized risk view. Each finding includes a risk score, the service it relates to, the affected resources it was observed on, a link to mitigation guidance, and the endpoint-specific evidence behind it. This enables you to see why a finding was raised on one machine and not another before deciding what to do. Most administrators work in AI Findings day to day and drop into AI Services for the full picture of a particular tool. A score of 0 means AI Visibility and Control found nothing risky in how a tool is configured, not that your organization approved it. Review AI Services against your list of sanctioned tools, not just AI Findings. Consider a developer who connects their AI assistant to the company ticketing system using a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which is a small connector that gives a model access to external tools. The setup requires only a few lines in a configuration file: there is no installer, no entry in the installed programs list, and no network traffic for controls to inspect. It simply surfaces in AI Services alongside the assets it exposes. The finding answers not just whether the connector exists, but what it reaches. A connector tied to a read-only reporting view presents a vastly different risk from one holding write credentials to a production database. This distinction lives entirely in its configuration. Meanwhile, the affected-host list clarifies the broader scope: whether this is an isolated shortcut or a pattern copied across the entire team. That endpoint-specific evidence is also what makes findings usable by a SOC analyst rather than only as a posture metric. A finding tied to a local model runtime or an MCP server identifies a process executing on a specific host outside the browser sandbox, and the affected-resources list gives the host set to pivot from, in Search and Incident Advisor. From Inventory to Enforcement GravityZone AI Visibility and Control establishes which AI is present and what about its configuration is risky. The score orders your queue; it does not decide the outcome. A high score is not an order to remove the tool, and a score of 0 is not an approval. It does not block access, remove software, or modify program permissions. Those actions are handled separately by existing controls within the GravityZone console. Blocking access to a prohibited service is Web Content Filtering. Most AI services are accessed through the browser, so once AIVC identifies which ones are in use, you block the domains. Blocking a specific tool wherever it turns up is what custom detection rules do: once AIVC has named the tool, you define a rule that matches it on process name, attach Kill process as an automatic action, and every later appearance is handled without an administrator in the loop, and is company-wide or scoped to endpoints carrying a given tag. Reducing what an installed tool is permitted to do belongs to hardening policies and to PHASR. PHASR for AI agents evaluates the agent separately from the person using the machine: processes started by a known agent binary are attributed to that agent's own behavioral profile rather than to the user's session, so the agent gets the tools its tasks require while the user's restrictions stay tied to the user's role. Turning on AI Visibility and Control does not require a rollout project. It runs on your existing Bitdefender Endpoint Security Tools agent and can be enabled by editing a current policy. The setting sits in the General section under Risk Management and applies to all endpoints targeted by that policy. Results will appear after the next risk scan. Summary Bitdefender GravityZone AI Visibility and Control provides the AI inventory your traditional software inventory cannot: browser-reached assistants, editor extensions, local runtimes, MCP servers, and agent frameworks; each with a risk score, one of 17 functional categories, and a list of impacted endpoints. It covers more 50 agents and 70,000 skills, and it records what is present and how it is configured, rather than user prompts. The two console views align with your existing workflow: AI Findings highlight what to address first, while AI Services gives a complete picture of any specific tool. A risk score tells you how exposed a tool is, not whether it is sanctioned; that decision, and the enforcement that follows, stays with you. Enforcement remains where it already lives: Web Content Filtering, custom detection rules, and PHASR, so your policy decisions stop being guesses, and you can gain greater confidence in the control you have over AI use within your organization.

14o8sns.text: Attackers took remote control of fridges and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets on the night of October 11 and warmed them, forcing stores to throw food away, several retail chains said. The attackers reached them through the controller that runs all of a store's fridges and freezers, a device made by Danish company Danfoss that maintenance firms can manage remotely. Les Mousquetaires, which owns the Intermarché chain, said its fridges and freezers were put into defrost and heated to as much as 50°C. CERT-FR, the French government's computer emergency response team, said in an alert published in French on October 12 that it is aware of numerous compromises affecting two Danfoss controller series, the AK-SM and the AK-SC. It told operators to disconnect the controllers or filter access to them. CERT-FR is part of ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency. ANSSI's head, Vincent Strubel, called it urgent to take the two series off the internet or filter access very tightly, AFP reported. Neither French authorities nor Danfoss has so far said who carried out the attack or how the attackers got into the controllers. Danfoss said most of the units hit were older models that it no longer updates. Which Chains Were Hit The chains gave their own figures to AFP, Reuters and broadcaster RTL. Each counts the stores the attack reached. Retailer Stores Reported Hit Source Intermarché and Netto (Les Mousquetaires) At least 300 across both brands, per AFP. About 150 stores, per Reuters Company statements, October 12 Coopérative U 80 of 2,000 Chief executive Dominique Schelcher, on RTL, October 13 Carrefour 80 supermarkets Company statements to AFP and Reuters, October 12 Monoprix About 30 Company statement to AFP, October 12 E.Leclerc Several stores Company statement to AFP, October 12 A store on that list did not always lose its stock. Schelcher told RTL that the cold chain held in most of the 80 Coopérative U stores hit, and that only a minority could not react fast enough and lost goods, according to AFP. He praised the quick reaction of store staff and refrigeration contractors. Intermarché, by contrast, said its affected stores had to throw away all the products concerned. Thierry Cotillard, who heads Les Mousquetaires, told broadcaster BFMTV he expected losses of tens of millions of euros across France, according to Reuters. In its statements on October 12, Danfoss gave no figure for how many systems were hit. It told Reuters it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems." Which Controllers, and Whether They Can Be Patched Danfoss told AFP that most of the units hit were older products that no longer get software or security updates, and it named two: the AK-SM 800 and the AK-SC 355. Danfoss declared the AK-SM 800 end-of-life in May 2021 and phased out the AK-SC 355 in 2016. In an October 2025 newsletter, it said it would end all services for such older products and urged customers to plan replacements. Some units of the current model, the AK-SM 800A, were also hit. Those were running outdated firmware, according to Danfoss's statement to trade publication Cooling Post, which did not name the versions. Controller Status, According to Danfoss Advice From CERT-FR and Danfoss AK-SM 800 End of life since May 2021. No software or security updates Disconnect it or filter access. Danfoss urges replacement AK-SC 355 Phased out in 2016. No software or security updates Disconnect it or filter access. Danfoss urges replacement AK-SM 800A Current model. Package 5.3.x, dated October 2026, was the latest listed on October 13 Disconnect it or filter access. Danfoss advises keeping firmware up to date As of October 13, Danfoss's security advisories page listed no advisory about the attack or about either older model. What Operators Should Do CERT-FR's first instruction covers every AK-SM and AK-SC controller: disconnect it or filter access to it. Exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice, the alert says. Where remote administration cannot be avoided, limiting access to trusted IP addresses is a first, temporary step. Beyond that, the alert advises following CERT-FR's hardening recommendations, which were written for the energy and water sector. Where a controller may have been compromised, the alert lists six steps, in this order: Limit network access to the controllers to service providers only. Do a factory reset. Apply all available security fixes. Change the device's secrets, such as passwords. Check the existing accounts. Reconfigure the device completely. Danfoss no longer issues fixes for the AK-SM 800 and the AK-SC 355, so the third step offers their owners no new fix. For the AK-SM 800A, the latest software package Danfoss listed on October 13 was 5.3.x. A system on version 3.x should move to 4.x first, and a controller cannot be downgraded once it runs 5.3.x, according to the package's readme. Starting with version 4.0, a setting called Strict Session Control is enabled by default and makes HTTPS mandatory. Danfoss's pages do not say whether the 5.3.x package was released in response to the attack. Danfoss told Cooling Post it was working with customers on "firmware updates where available, stronger network protections and removing direct internet exposure where applicable." Its general security guidance, published in French, also tells operators to keep controllers unreachable from the internet, change default passwords when a system is installed, and require remote users to log in through a single managed entry point. CERT-FR had published no indicators of compromise as of October 13, so operators have no official signs to check for. Coopérative U's stores do not buy directly from Danfoss. They are customers of refrigeration contractors that supply them with the Danfoss system, Schelcher said. How the Attackers Got In Is Not Established As of October 13, CERT-FR had named no vulnerability, no firmware version, and no way in. Its alert warns against exposing management interfaces to the internet without saying that was the route. A person close to French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told AFP that ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and had contacted the vendor. No CVE was named, and the statement does not say the vulnerability was used in the attack. E.Leclerc told AFP that a cyberattack had affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers, with effects on cold equipment in several of its stores. The supplier was not named. Danfoss issued fixes for three flaws in the newer AK-SM 800A in 2025. Neither French authorities nor Danfoss has linked them to this attack. CVE-2025-41450 is an authentication bypass, a way past the login, in versions before 4.2. CVE-2025-41451 is a command injection flaw that could lead to remote code execution, and CVE-2025-41452 could allow a denial-of-service attack. Both need a login and were fixed in version 4.3.1. Researchers at Claroty described the three flaws in August, said they could be combined into attack chains, and reported finding thousands of AK-SM 800A management interfaces reachable from the internet. Their tests of the flaws were laboratory work on the newer model. The report describes no attacks and does not mention the two older models. Danfoss's October 2025 newsletter records earlier attacks on the AK-SM 800: 16 Russian supermarkets using the model were targeted in 2022, and 40 Israeli stores were hacked the same year. All 40 lacked proper firewall or VPN protection, and the newsletter names no vulnerability in either case. The Inquiry and Reports From Other Countries The Paris prosecutor's office has opened an inquiry on its own initiative, it told AFP. Its cybercrime section leads the inquiry, which is assigned to the anti-cybercrime office known as OFAC. The inquiry is to count the victims and establish the link between the attack and the damage they reported, which includes lost food and equipment that began to catch fire. ANSSI is in contact with cybersecurity agencies in other European countries because those countries may be affected, the person close to the Prime Minister said. Félix Aimé, a senior threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia, told Reuters that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected. Reuters gave no details on those cases.

vzl6n6.text: Two of 31 newly disclosed flaws in Progress Software's MarkLogic Server database could let an account given only some management privileges take administrator control of the server, the company says. Progress published all 31 on October 12 and scored five of them critical. Fixes have been available since September 10, in MarkLogic 11.3.7 and MarkLogic 12.1.0. Affected releases, and the release that fixes each: MarkLogic 11.x before 11.3.7: upgrade to 11.3.7 MarkLogic 12.x before 12.1.0: upgrade to 12.1.0 MarkLogic 11.3 is the long-term support (LTS) line. The 12 line, which Progress calls an innovation release, has no patched 12.0 release. Its fix is 12.1.0, which also adds new features. Installing the fixes for the 10 MarkLogic flaws Progress disclosed in August is not enough. Those fixes arrived in 11.3.6 and 12.0.3, and both releases are affected by the new flaws. Progress's CVE records and its upgrade notes for the two releases do not say whether any of the 31 flaws has been used in attacks. None was in the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog when The Hacker News checked on October 13. The same records and notes list no workaround for customers who cannot upgrade yet. What the Critical Flaws Allow Progress scored three of the five critical flaws 9.9 out of 10 on the CVSS scale and the other two 9.6. For each one, the attacker must already have a privilege or a way to run code on the server, according to the company's CVE records. Two of them involve forests. In MarkLogic, a forest is a collection of documents that is attached to a database. CVE Score What the Attacker Needs What It Could Allow CVE-2026-85947 9.9 Forest-management privileges Create a persistent administrator account, potentially giving complete administrative control of the server CVE-2026-85948 9.9 Manage-user-level privileges Gain persistent administrative control, through an XQuery injection flaw in a deprecated Management API path CVE-2026-85955 9.9 Query-execution access and the xdmp-eval-in privilege Run server-side code with elevated permissions CVE-2026-85956 9.6 Delegated database-administrator privileges Back up or restore forests outside its own database, allowing access to or changes to what Progress calls "security-critical data" CVE-2026-9191 9.6 The ability to run code through certain REST and XDBC evaluation paths Perform unauthorized actions or compromise an authenticated session The fix for CVE-2026-85947 shows which accounts are at issue. A "forest-scoped administrative grant" is no longer enough on its own to attach a forest to a database of the account's choosing, the upgrade notes say. They also tell customers to review delegated forest and database privilege assignments before upgrading, and to audit the roles that hold xdmp-eval-in. Outside researchers reported four of the five through Bugcrowd. A researcher using the handle rexnets is credited with CVE-2026-85947, CVE-2026-85948, and CVE-2026-85956, and another using the handle WaltWhitehat is credited with CVE-2026-9191. Flaws That Depend on Configuration Progress scored 24 of the remaining flaws high and two medium. The highest, CVE-2026-85954, at 8.6, could allow an attacker to gain more privileges than granted by passing values to certain XQuery functions. Several of the others apply only where a named feature or platform is in use: SAML: In deployments that use SAML authentication, an unauthenticated remote attacker could make the server accept an assertion it should reject (CVE-2026-85962). On 11.x, the SAML parser could also process external DTDs or entities (CVE-2026-85957). OAuth: An attacker could use a token that the server should not accept (CVE-2026-85958). The fix adds issuer and audience checks for Ping Identity and other OAuth configurations. Password-based Kerberos: In certain configurations, an attacker positioned on the network could impersonate the Kerberos authentication service (CVE-2026-85972). Cloud hosting: An authenticated attacker could access internal cloud services and obtain cloud credentials on Azure (CVE-2026-85951) and on Linux-based cloud deployments (CVE-2026-85952). Diagnostic logs: Under certain configurations, the server could write security-sensitive information to diagnostic logs (CVE-2026-85949 and, on Azure, CVE-2026-85961). AWS secret keys and session tokens were written in plaintext when the affected IAM trace path was enabled, the upgrade notes say. Amazon S3: Connections to S3 could use cleartext by default (CVE-2026-85975). Query Console: A remote attacker who gets a logged-in Query Console user to open a malicious page could run server-side code with that user's permissions (CVE-2026-85960). An authenticated Query Console user could read arbitrary server files (CVE-2026-85964). Legacy components: OpsDirector, a deprecated feature, could let an unauthenticated remote attacker make requests to internal services or forge trusted requests (CVE-2026-85963). Legacy InfoStudio modules could give access to server files (CVE-2026-85953). The rest include three memory-safety flaws, a cross-site scripting flaw, HTTP response splitting in Query Console, inconsistent TLS hostname checks on some outbound connections, and cleartext cluster-management traffic on 12.x. What the Upgrade Changes Progress tells customers to read its upgrade notes, the known incompatibilities for 11.3.7 and those for 12.1.0, before upgrading. The 11.3.7 notes list behavior changes tied to 22 of the flaws, and the 12.1.0 notes to 21. Changes that can break existing code, tools, or automation include: mlcp: Older versions of MarkLogic Content Pump (mlcp) fail against the new releases with an XDMP-ISOLATED error. Progress recommends mlcp 11.3.7 or 12.1.0. Older versions can run with -restrict_hosts set to true, which can reduce performance. Removed features: The /manage/v2/packages API, InfoStudio, and OpsDirector are removed. New defaults: XML external entity processing is off by default, S3 connections default to HTTPS, and new and rotated ErrorLog.txt and AuditLog.txt files are created with mode 0640 instead of 0666. Privileges: xdmp:eval-in() now needs both the xdmp-eval-in and xdmp-eval privileges. Reading Authorization headers needs a new privilege that no built-in role holds. Forest attachment, backup and restore are checked against every forest and database they touch. Stored secrets: FlexRep configuration responses no longer return stored passwords, client private keys or passphrases. Platform: MarkLogic 11.3.7 does not support Amazon Linux 2. Name conflicts: The upgrade can fail if the cluster already has a role, user or privilege with one of five names used by a new ticket system. The names are in the upgrade notes. Changes with no CVE attached: Both releases limit XML entity expansion and drop weak TLS ciphers from the defaults. On 12.1.0, Optic fragment queries return only document fragments by default. On the fix for CVE-2026-85954, the notes warn: "As a result, you may no longer have privileges that you previously had access to, because that access was incorrect." Some problems remain after the upgrade. Existing ErrorLog.txt and AuditLog.txt files keep their old permissions until they are rotated or recreated. The Kerberos fix needs a keytab, and without one, the server logs a warning and skips the new check. Another flaw, CVE-2026-85959, meant successful logins were not always recorded in the audit log. Progress says that could limit a customer's ability to detect and investigate unauthorized access or credential misuse. The CVE records and upgrade notes do not say whether upgrading removes an administrator account created through CVE-2026-85947 before the upgrade. Second Batch Since August The 31 flaws are the second batch Progress has disclosed for MarkLogic in 68 days. On August 5, it published 10, seven of them scored critical. One, CVE-2026-9192, was scored 9.8 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass password verification on the ODBC App Server, according to its CVE record. Both times the fixes shipped first. The August flaws were fixed in releases dated July 1 and July 6, 35 and 30 days before their CVE records appeared. This time the gap was 32 days. A search by The Hacker News of the U.S. National Vulnerability Database (NVD) on October 13 returned 49 CVE records that mention MarkLogic, 41 of them from these two batches. The other eight, from 2017 and 2018, are for Antenna House DMC HTMLFilter, a third-party component used by MarkLogic 8.0-6. Earlier MarkLogic releases also carried security fixes: the release notes for 11.3.1, 11.3.2 and 11.3.4 each mention "patches for security vulnerabilities" and name no CVE in the server's own code.

1514jxr.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 13, 2026Vulnerability / DevSecOps GitLab has released patches for a maximum-severity security flaw impacting its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) software that could result in arbitrary code execution. "GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation," the company said in a Monday advisory. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229, has been described as an integer overflow issue. It carries a CVSS score of 10.0. It affects the following versions - All versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8 All versions from 19.3 before 19.3.5, and All versions from 19.4 before 19.4.2 Patches for the flaw are available in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8. Also addressed are three high-severity bugs - CVE-2026-92883 (CVSS score: 8.7) - A cross-site scripting vulnerability that could allow an authenticated user to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of other users' browser sessions via a specially crafted repository. CVE-2026-16301 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper authorization vulnerability in the downstream pipeline creation service that could allow an authenticated user with Developer role to execute CI/CD pipelines on protected branches. CVE-2026-14814 (CVSS score: 8.2) - A permissive regular expression vulnerability that could allow a user to poison cached responses for raw repository files, causing targeted users’ CI/CD pipelines to execute specially crafted content and potentially exposing protected environment variables. The disclosure comes weeks after it remediated a critical flaw in AI Gateway (CVE-2026-90970, CVSS score: 9.9) that could have allowed an authenticated user with Duo Agent Platform access to break out of the prompt template sandbox via a specially crafted flow configuration and achieve arbitrary command execution on the AI Gateway. Last month, another maximum-severity security flaw in GitLab CE and EE (CVE-2026-85706, CVSS score: 10.0) witnessed in-the-wild probes within hours of public disclosure.

tax0ge.text: Low-cost Android smartphones have been shipped with malicious software baked into the device firmware, allowing bad actors to covertly install apps, conduct ad fraud, and turn devices into residential proxies. The activity, which targets Android devices built on MediaTek platforms across several brands, is being tracked by Bitdefender under the moniker Midnight Mimosa. The preinstalled malware ("com.android.system.lite") runs with system-level privileges, which make it possible to install or uninstall apps, grant itself additional permissions to accessibility services, notifications, and SMS, and load arbitrary code supplied remotely by the operators. Specifically, it fetches a remote configuration from an external server and then downloads and executes additional payloads designed to conduct ad fraud and silent installation or removal of partner apps. These apps incorporate proxyware, ad fraud, and code execution features. It can also grant permission to any Android app package. "This essentially means its operators could install and delete apps at will, tuning each device to their needs, including making them part of large botnets," the Romanian cybersecurity company said. "This scheme is likely designed mainly to generate revenue. The operators carry out ad and click fraud, collect device and installed-app information, and turn infected devices into residential-proxy relay nodes, making them zombies in botnets." It's worth emphasizing that the malware itself doesn't engage in fraudulent clicks. Instead, the monetization effort is driven by dropper apps that masquerade as seemingly harmless utility apps, which are responsible for loading genuine ads through a legitimate advertising software development kit (SDK). The end goal is to load an invisible window on top of apps that registers the ads being shown. In all, Bitdefender said it discovered 13 apps on Google Play that communicate with the same servers that control the malware, indicating the campaign is not limited to preinstalled firmware - com.audify.editor.wavrge appicon.diy.tools.prop com.audify.editor.pro com.prorestore.qr com.message.recovery.prorestore com.go.weather.mot com.cool.weather.yl com.dmstudio.weather com.dl.guard.lock picturetranslate.extractor.text.lite com.notemaster.record.mark com.arabmusic.tap.aghani_tamerhosny org.life.goal.tools A notable aspect of the malware is that it disables the Google Play Store app prior to installing a payload app, likely in an attempt to bypass Play Protect safeguards, and then re-enable the app after the payload is run. What's more, the malware has been detected on devices with firmware signed using certificates attributed to Shenzhen Zediel Co., Ltd, a Chinese Android device manufacturer. However, it's unclear at this stage if the certificate owner was involved in or aware of the malware deployment. However, Bitdefender noted that it also detected other company names over the course of its investigation. The preinstalled nature of the malware suggests a compromise of the device supply chain, with Bitdefender highlighting some level of infrastructure overlaps with Android.Phantom, which was documented by Doctor Web as bundled within modded games and popular apps to conduct click fraud. The vast majority of the infected devices are located in Mexico, followed by France, Italy, the U.S., Germany, Brazil, Spain, the U.K., Canada, Romania, Poland, and Thailand. This is not the first time a firmware-level backdoor has been observed targeting Android devices. Late last year, Kaspersky disclosed details of another malware codenamed Keenadu that was discovered preinstalled on certain models of tablets running Android to primarily enable ad fraud. "Preinstalled malware is a different threat class," Bitdefender said. "Every user-facing defense assumes the owner is in the loop at installation: the install prompt, the store review, Play Protect, and the ability to uninstall afterwards." "Remediation cannot rely on uninstall. Because the root component ships in the system partition, an affected owner cannot remove it by the normal route. Clearing the device requires firmware-level cleanup or disabling the component over ADB, and neither is realistic for most people who own these phones. The durable fix sits with the vendors and the marketplaces that ship and sell the affected firmware."

hg3opt.text: Norway’s Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) has fined Xandr, a Microsoft-owned advertising company, $9.6M (NOK 92 million) for unlawfully processing and sharing sensitive data belonging to Grindr users in the country. The data protection authority said this is the largest fine it has ever issued. “We issued such a high fine in this case because the breaches we identified were very serious,” said Line Coll, Director General of Datatilsynet. “Thousands of users in Norway have been subjected to unlawful sharing of their sensitive data.” According to the authority’s findings, between July 2018 and April 2020, Xandr managed real-time advertising auctions inside Grindr that potentially exposed users’ data, including sensitive sexual orientation information, to thousands of companies. These auctions work by advertisers bidding for the right to display an ad to a Grindr user after they receive profiling information from Xandr, which acted as the intermediary. At the time, Xandr was a joint controller with Grindr, meaning it was responsible for how the data was used and should have required and obtained explicit consent from the data subjects for this processing. Grindr is a location-based dating app primarily serving the LGBTQ+ community. According to Norway's data privacy agency, Xandr assumed Grindr had obtained valid consent but did not take any action to verify it. “Xandr omitted to verify that the consents from Grindr were valid, and did not do anything to ensure they had a legal basis for their own processing,” Coll stated. As a result, sensitive information about Grindr users from Norway and other countries was exposed to thousands of advertisers without the users realizing it, or ever providing explicit consent. Austrian nonprofit privacy rights organization Noyb, which filed the original complaint in January 2020, together with the Norwegian Consumer Council (Forbrukerrådet), applauded the Datatilsynet decision, calling it “a major blow to the online adtech industry.” According to the organization, the decision puts a brake to the bad practices of large players in the online advertising and commercial surveillance industry, including the unrestricted and covert exchange of sensitive user data between websites, apps, platforms, and operating systems. “The current fine shows that companies such as Xandr are eventually held accountable for their shady practices,” Noyb said. “Profiling people’s interests, habits, location, and behavior requires valid consent – which adtech companies hardly ever obtain.” Xandr, which now operates as Microsoft Advertising, was given three weeks to appeal the decision. BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft for a comment on the Norwegian agency's decision, and a spokesperson underlined that the investigation and the outcome "focused on conduct that predates Microsoft's acquisition of Xandr." Since then, legal frameworks and the way they are interpreted and enforced have changed, the spokesperson said, adding that Microsoft is "reviewing the decision and assessing our options."
