ncz4xc.text: Russian cloud services provider Yandex announced that drone attacks damaged three of its data centers, forcing it to shut down two facilities and partially disable a third. Yandex customers are experiencing service outages, some of them reporting inability to access files stored on the company’s cloud infrastructure. The impacted data centers are in Sasovo (hit on October 8), Kaluga (hit on October 9), and Vladimir (attacked on October 11). The Sasovo and Vladimir facilities stopped operating completely, while the Kaluga facility's operations are degraded. The attacks are believed to have been carried out by Ukrainian forces trying to cause widespread operational disruptions. Yandex reported no injuries related to these incidents. As Russia’s largest technology companies, Yandex is often called “Russia’s Google,” offering search engine, maps, and navigation services. The company also offers ride-hailing, delivery, shopping, streaming, email, cloud storage, and business cloud infrastructure services. Much of the country's internet infrastructure, serving both government and private-sector organizations, relies on Yandex's services. EU MEP Tomáš Zdechovský highlighted a potential connection between Yandex outages and a sudden drop in communication from online accounts promoting far-right ideals in Germany. On its status page, Yandex said its teams are working around the clock to maintain services and help affected customers and partners, but it cannot provide a reliable service-restoration timeline. For this reason, Yandex urged customers to use alternative infrastructure for disaster recovery. “We consider the remaining resource configuration to be unstable,” reads one of Yandex’s status updates from yesterday. “The platform's operating mode is emergency – we recommend using any other alternative disaster recovery plans. Technical-supported communication channels can be unstable.” As of the most recent update, Yandex’s Console, API, IAM, Container Registry, databases, S3 storage, and Kubernetes were available, with some performance or availability issues. Compute, AI Studio, and security services were partially available, while Monium is still offline. One Yandex customer reported issues starting on October 8, with backups to their Yandex Disk missing thumbnails and an inability to download previously submitted files. Failure to fetch file contentsSource: habr.com The user reports getting HTTP 302 redirects, HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout errors, and HTTP 500 errors when trying to access or work on the files. It is currently unclear whether any data stored in the affected data centers has been irreversibly lost, as Yandex has not addressed the problem in its status updates. 2q6q9g.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 12, 2026Cybersecurity News / Hacking Some meetings last longer than it took attackers to jump on a newly disclosed security flaw this week. Within hours, they were already testing it. That's not much time to read the warning, let alone do something about it. But speed is only part of the problem. A secure connection didn't always mean a safe destination. People offering to fix a ransomware mess had questions to answer themselves. Malware got better at hiding its tracks. And some systems turned out to be easier to break into than anyone would like to admit. The odd part is how normal much of it looked until someone checked closer. There's more going on here than a few bad bugs and clever attacks. Some of the smaller stories are just as telling. This week's full recap is worth a read, especially the bits that didn't make the big headlines. ⚡ Threat of the Week Atlassian Flaw Exploited in the Wild — Threat actors have begun to exploit a newly disclosed critical security flaw impacting Atlassian Data Center products that could allow access to sensitive files under certain conditions. The arbitrary file access flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-21589 (CVSS score: 9.3) affects multiple products, including Bitbucket Data Center, Confluence Data Center, Jira Service Management Data Center, Jira Software Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible, and Fisheye. The exploitation activity targeting its honeypot network is said to have begun two hours after watchTowr released additional technical details of the vulnerability. 🔔 Top News Ransomware Recovery CEO Charged for Secretly Paying Hackers — Zohar Pinhasi, the owner of Florida-based ransomware recovery firm MonsterCloud, was hit with wire fraud charges for allegedly falsely claiming he could help victims restore data without paying ransoms. Instead, prosecutors said Pinhasi simply paid ransoms and charged victims a fee that was significantly higher than the original ransom demand. MonsterCloud was also highlighted in a 2019 ProPublica investigation on companies defrauding ransomware victims by paying ransoms and charging exorbitant fees. New DarkSword Variant Detected — A previously unseen variant of the DarkSword iOS exploit kit called P7 DarkSword has been updated to support on-device keychain and crypto-wallet theft, and facilitate two-way C2 communication with the attacker's infrastructure. The new variant is much better at hiding itself and cleaning up its behavior, rendering previous indicators of compromise (IOCs) ineffective. The changes indicate substantial work by the operators rather than simple modifications. The most important change is that it can extract Keychain data directly on the iPhone before sending it to the attackers, as opposed to copying the entire Keychain database for processing remotely. Evidence indicates that the exploit kit is distributed via malicious ads as part of watering hole attacks. UAC-0099 Continues to Update MATCHBOIL Malware — The Russia-aligned threat actor known as UAC-0099 is actively refining a malware downloader called MATCHBOIL, suggesting it intends to use the tool in future attacks. Over the past year, MATCHBOIL has evolved from a dropper that essentially executed once, contacted its C2 server, and downloaded and installed a next-stage payload, into one that's run every two minutes. The change allows it to repeatedly contact its control server and fetch new or updated payloads. FBI Disrupts Hacking Tools and Domains Linked to Flax Typhoon — The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Department of Justice (DoJ) announced the disruption of malicious tools used by a China-linked advanced persistent threat group known as Flax Typhoon. While Microscan was used to conduct reconnaissance and computer vulnerability scanning, FishHub allegedly enabled the exploitation of computer networks through spear-phishing attacks and the deployment of follow-on payloads. CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity, Chris Butera, said Chinese government hackers "continue to position themselves within critical infrastructure networks, including operational technology (OT) systems, with the aim of disrupting critical functions at a future time of their choosing." Integrity Technology is best known in China for developing the country's cyber ranges and has publicly touted its extensive government funding in the past. Natto Thoughts research said the company was founded in 2010 by Cai Jingjing, a legendary hacker in China. Another ShinyHunters Arrest Made — FBI said it made a third arrest in connection with the ShinyHunters group, as the net closes around the notorious cybercrime group. "Our agents in the field have arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group – the group believed to be responsible for the recent FBIjobs.gov incident, which occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor," FBI director Kash Patel said. Although the identity of the individual was not disclosed, court documents, POLITICO, and independent security journalist Brian Krebs said it was Edward Dubrovsky, a 54-year-old cybersecurity executive and investor based in Toronto. Dubrovsky has been charged with conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats. It is the third publicly announced arrest since news of ‌the ⁠breach came out in late September 2026. In a Telegram post, the group said, "We will not remain active on Telegram for much longer, as several of our members have reportedly been arrested by the FBI." Attackers Hijack Three ccTLDs to Obtain Google Certificates — Google said unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates for several Google domains and hijacked domains in the country-code top-level domains (ccTLDs) for Ghana (.gh), American Samoa (.as), and Sierra Leone (.sl) after compromising third-party operators and modifying authoritative DNS records. "During these hijacks, attackers modified authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering several Google domains, as well as domains belonging to other organizations," Google said. "Following our initial mitigation, Certificate Transparency (CT) log data revealed additional organizations, including several leading global brands and widely used online services, believed to have been impacted by the same attacks." Chrome blocked the unauthorized certificates through CRLSets. GoBalance Flaw Can Be Used to Hijack TOR .onion Sites — A vulnerability in GoBalance, a load-balancing tool used by many darknet sites, can be abused to recover a site's master signing scalar from its publicly available data, ultimately enabling site takeover and redirection. "Between 5 and 7 October, both onion addresses of Dread, a prominent darknet forum, were taken over and redirected to a rival platform, Conclave," Searchlight Cyber said. "Several marketplaces using the same software were also affected. Dread's operators initially attributed the incident to an accidental key leak; the evidence set out below indicates that the GoBalance flaw was the more likely cause, at least for the second address." ‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild. Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-86360, CVE-2026-86361, CVE-2026-86362 (Dell System Update), CVE-2026-21589 (Atlassian), CVE-2026-93355 (LiteLLM), CVE-2026-106382, CVE-2026-106197, CVE-2026-106358, CVE-2026-106347 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-102255 (SonicWall SMA 1000), CVE-2026-105192 (LMCache), CVE-2026-102406, CVE-2026-103008, CVE-2026-102404, CVE-2026-102413 (Elasticsearch), CVE-2026-104711, CVE-2026-104712, CVE-2026-104713, CVE-2026-104714 (Apache Struts), CVE-2026-91140 (Progress DataDirect), CVE-2025-64393, CVE-2026-58069 (Veeam Backup & Replication), CVE-2026-32740 (Next.js), CVE-2026-18397 (Thales SConnect), CVE-2026-84388 (Fortinet FortiPAM Chrome extension), CVE-2026-76464, CVE-2026-20328, CVE-2026-76454, CVEs, CVE-2026-76482, CVE-2026-76480, CVE-2026-76483, CVE-2026-76455, CVE-2026-76459, CVE-2026-76471, CVE-2026-76465, CVE-2026-76485, CVE-2026-76486, CVE-2026-76501, CVE-2026-76498, CVE-2026-76499, CVE-2026-76500 (Cisco), CVE-2026-76281, CVE-2026-76282, CVE-2026-76284, CVE-2026-76268 (Splunk), CVE-2026-85097 (Bricksforge WordPress plugin), CVE-2026-93836 (WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce WordPress plugin), CVE-2026-94504 (Ninja Forms WordPress plugin), CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134 (AhsayCBS), CVE-2026-96940 (Microsoft Exchange Server), CVE-2026-63277 (LibreOffice), CVE-2026-59265 (Apache OpenOffice), and multiple vulnerabilities in WordPress. 🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars AI Attacks Move at Machine Speed. Can Your Identity Security Keep Up? → AI-powered attacks can now move from reconnaissance to privilege escalation faster than traditional security teams can investigate and respond. This webinar explains why identity is becoming the critical real-time control layer—and how runtime identity security can help organizations detect risky access, enforce decisions across cloud, SaaS, on-prem, and AI environments, and stop machine-speed attacks before they turn into breaches. AI Agents Have Too Much Access — Learn How to Control the Risk → AI agents are moving fast inside organizations, often with access to sensitive data, credentials, and business systems before security teams have full visibility or control. This webinar breaks down how shadow AI creates insider risk and shows how to govern AI access, reduce exposure, and enable safer adoption without slowing the business. 📰 Around the Cyber World The India-nexus adversary known as Dropping Elephant (aka Patchwork) has been observed targeting government, defense, naval, aerospace/UAV, academic, and other strategically significant sectors across Pakistan, Sri Lanka, China, and South Korea. "The group continues to use spear-phishing campaigns with malicious LNK attachments to deliver PowerShell-based malware, DLL sideloading payloads, and in-memory RAT," Arctic Wolf said. Bitter, another threat actor assessed to be operating with interests aligned to India, targeted a European embassy in Asia in June 2026 with a spear-phishing email bearing a FIFA World Cup-themed lure to deliver BDarkRAT. "The attackers compromised a legitimate mailbox belonging to a diplomatic account from an African country to send the malicious message," Trellix said. "The attack utilized a multistage delivery method beginning with a ZIP file attachment containing a VHDX disk image. Inside this image lay a shortcut (.lnk) masquerading as a PDF document. Upon execution, this shortcut initiated an obfuscated PowerShell and command-line sequence. This process established a scheduled task, deceptively named to appear like a system error to ensure persistence, and beaconed to a remote server. This initial connection facilitated reconnaissance by gathering system information and eventually downloading a second-stage MSI installer, which deployed the BDarkRAT remote-access trojan." Let's Encrypt said TLS certificate lifetimes are dropping from 90 to 64 days by default starting February 2027, in preparation for 45-day lifetimes planned for 2028. In a lengthy post on X, Microsoft's CEO Satya Nadella called out the dangers posed by highly advanced AI models, stating AI can no longer be treated as a "set of nested black boxes" and urged building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leave behind "tamper-proof human-readable evidence." Nadella added, "We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start. Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task. More advanced models will require more advanced containment technologies that we need to standardize on." Data from Comparitech showed that Q3 2026 saw the highest quarterly figures to date for ransomware attacks, with 2,627 incidents reported in total. This represents a 29% increase from Q2 2026, when 2,030 attacks were recorded and a 61% increase from Q3 2025, when 1,636 attacks took place. The median ransomware demand was $150,000 and the average was $602,400. The most prolific gangs were Qilin and The Gentlemen. Oleg Korniev, 42, a dual citizen of Ukraine and Russia, pleaded guilty in the U.S. to running a sophisticated international money laundering organization that laundered millions of dollars stolen from U.S. victims. The criminal organization recruited over 15,000 U.S.-based money mules to launder at least $10 million stolen by hackers from over 750 U.S. bank accounts. Korniev was one of the leaders of Your Mule Cashout (YMCO). A U.S. jury convicted Jonathan Spalletta (aka Cthulhon and Jspalletta), 36, of Maryland, of computer fraud and money laundering over two separate hacks of decentralized crypto exchange Uranium Finance in 2021. He faces up to 10 years in prison on the fraud count and 20 years on the money laundering count. "In the first hack, on April 8, 2021, Spalletta engaged in a deceptive series of transactions with Uranium's smart contract that Spalletta used to withdraw far more 'rewards' in cryptocurrency than he was authorized to receive," the Justice Department said. "He repeated those transactions over and over until he had drained the liquidity pool of nearly all its rewards tokens. In total, Spalletta successfully extracted cryptocurrency worth approximately $1.4 million in the first hack. In the second hack, on April 28, 2021, Spalletta exploited an error in the Uranium smart contract that governed how much cryptocurrency he could withdraw in a liquidity pool on Uranium. Spalletta exploited that issue across multiple separate Uranium liquidity pools, fraudulently obtaining approximately $53.3 million in cryptocurrency and causing Uranium to shut down due to lack of funds." The stolen funds were eventually laundered through a complex series of cryptocurrency transactions, including by using the cryptocurrency mixer Tornado Cash. OpenAI disclosed it disrupted two influence operations from Russia (Dark Clark) and Iran (Bogus Bylines) that used ChatGPT and other AI tools to create "false front" entities, such as seven fake journalist personas and covert think tanks, that successfully planted stories and narratives in mainstream news publications. "They used those entities to launder geopolitical, conflict-related messaging into their target audiences," OpenAI said. "Both operations were multi-dimensional, trying a range of different tactics to achieve their goals. As well as long-form articles, the Iranian operation generated batches of social media comments, generally on topics related to the US-Iran war. As well as controlling the 'think tank,' the Russian operation created fake 'leaked' documents and audio scripts, some of which we identified as being spread online." Some of the outlets that published the articles, however, had substantial audiences, including one with 2 million Facebook followers. Threat actors are embedding "AI-Analysis Evasion" (aka A3) capabilities in malware by embedding natural-language instructions to influence automated analysis. Such techniques have been detected against four malware families: FRUITSHELL, PLOTSAFE, HOLLOWCLAD, and MANTLEMAZE, per Cisco Talos. This includes anti-analysis comments in source code, in some cases generating them from a template and incorporating intimidation notes that instruct the model that it is a monitored honeypot. "What began as a direct-instruction technique has evolved to target multiple models through template spraying," Talos said. "Malware authors are also attempting to establish multiple analysis-bypass conditions by using direct or indirect deterrence instructions aimed at the model." A brand deal scam is targeting YouTube creators by impersonating Hollyland, a legitimate manufacturer of wireless transmission and audiovisual equipment. The phishing emails lead to a fake website that instructs them to sign in with their Google account with an aim to harvest their credentials. "The attackers who hijack your account could use it to access other linked services or impersonate them to contact your followers or collaborators," ESET said. "The compromised account can also be misused to spread malicious links and peddle other scams." A high-severity flaw in NVIDIA's DCGM Exporter GPU monitoring tool (CVE-2026-47483, CVSS score: 8.2) could be abused by unauthenticated attackers to flood its profiling endpoints with concurrent unauthenticated requests to exhaust resources and crash the service, potentially slowing AI workloads running on the same host. Lava Security said it found roughly 2,100 hosts exposing the exporter to the internet without authentication between March and May 2026, leaking telemetry data from more than 12,000 GPUs. The hosts belonged to about 300 organizations, with the GPUs representing about $100 million in hardware. The flaw has been addressed in version 4.8.2 or later. "As AI infrastructure scales, organizations need to protect every layer of the stack and know exactly what they are responsible for versus what their provider is responsible for," Lava said. Raheim Hamilton, 30, a Virginia man who co-created and operated Empire Market, a dark web marketplace that peddled illegal goods and services, was sentenced to 40 years in federal prison. Raheim pleaded guilty in January 2026. Three new malware loaders have been spotted in the wild: 2CLoader, which delivers Vidar, Remus Stealer, and XWorm RAT, AvisLoader, which is delivered via ClickFix lures and communicates via Fox, an encrypted peer-to-peer (P2P) messaging network, to fetch commands and additional payloads from the operator, and Sauron Loader, which offers loader-type functionality exclusively to Russian-speaking cybercriminals. Details have emerged about two Zammad flaws that were exploited as zero-days to breach the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD). According to Horizon3.ai and Sysdig, CVE-2026-102489 is a remote code execution flaw affecting versions 6.3.0 to 6.5.4, while CVE-2026-102490 is a local privilege escalation (LPE) flaw affecting all versions from 1.5.0 to 7.1.0-alpha. On October 2, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by October 5, 2026. An investigation into a September 2026 Akira ransomware attack undertaken by Huntress found that "the threat actor behind the attack accessed the endpoint via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), disabled antivirus, and deployed Rclone for data exfiltration, before deploying the ransomware. The actor also deployed a GOST tunneling tool, likely for persistence." Conclusion A few arrests and takedowns brought some good news this week. But the bigger picture is less comforting. Attackers keep finding new ways in, old mistakes still work, and even the systems meant to help or protect people aren't always what they seem. That's it for this edition. Not every story here needs your attention, but a few might deserve a closer look. Especially the ones that sound a little too familiar to your own setup. Better to spot the problem in someone else's story than become part of the next one. See you next week.

1rd86wb.text: The personal AI agents rollout is going about as smoothly as expected: Amazon now blocks Meta's Muse because it doesn't identify itself as a bot while browsing; Instinct keeps raising privacy concerns; and the horror stories from pretty much every personal AI agent keep piling up. Regardless, the tech world is mesmerized by the capabilities and potential of these services. Less than a year after the first release of the open-source agent now called OpenClaw, the juggernauts are putting their weight behind the idea that each of us needs a personal assistant. You know what's coming: your employees will connect their personal agents to work systems. There's no stopping that. Their agents already manage their home time, and managing their work time is the next logical step. For them, that is. Not for your security. Given that personal agents will reach corporate systems whether approved or not, you might be wondering what the best way is to block them. If that’s your thinking, we’re here to offer you another path: enable safe usage instead, with identity as the control plane, and reap the benefits. BYOD, meet BYOA(I) The Bring-Your-Own-Device shift is the obvious comparison, but calling this the new era of BYOD would undersell the challenges personal AI agents introduce. These aren't just devices presumed to be insecure that contain company data, but entire AIs that act on company systems in the employee’s name. Bring-Your-Own-AI (or Bring-Your-Own-Agent) is, then, an identity challenge first and foremost. The best-case scenario is an agent wielding identities with an owner of record, limited approval, and no offboarding. You will also have agents who pretend to be employees, and agents with identities that have no easily recognizable owner. But the main difference between the two movements is where the control point sits. BYOD gave IT a device to enroll. A personal agent is something you can't register: it lives on the vendor's computer or blends into the employee's. And it's likely in your systems today, whether you can see it or not. How personal agents get in Whoever connects a personal AI agent to your systems today likely does this without ever filing a ticket. Instead, they connect it the way they'd connect other apps: OAuth consent. The agent requests access to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or Slack, and the employee clicks Allow. If your tenant lets users consent to third-party apps, that's the whole process. A text thread. Take Instinct, for example. Users text it, link their Google, Apple, or Facebook account, and it acts through the services they connect. Saved passwords in the agent's browser. Many of the agents can sign in to supported sites using passwords via a browser and an internal password manager. To your app, it looks like the employee is logging in. API keys and personal access tokens. For unofficial integrations, many agents can use API keys and personal access tokens, which require users to create long-term credentials. The employee's own laptop. A local agent like OpenClaw reaches whatever the machine it's installed on can see. Muse got a Mac app on September 18 that reads files, notes, calendars, and email with the user's permission, and can take optional Full Disk Access. Dots can work from the user's laptop once it's connected. The same goes for AI browsers like Atlassian's Dia, which read your open pages and connect to Slack and Gmail. Meet the agents Less than a year into the category, we’re already starting to see sub-categories emerge in the nascent personal AI agent market. Some agents are more corporate, and others are more personal. But you’ll be hard-pressed to find one that’s truly tailored to a work environment in terms of what it does, and, more importantly, doesn’t do. Take OpenAI’s Dots, for example. It’s as corporate as a product such as this can be. “Specialist dots” will have their own identities and credentials. OpenAI is working with Microsoft to deploy them under Agent 365, and the connectors are based on those created for ChatGPT. Even the rollout is limited to enterprise accounts and high-tier subscriptions. xAI’s GrokBot has an R&D distribution channel via Cursor. If your devs have Cursor, they might have access to GrokBot. Here, the idea is to turn the AI bot tied to the work-controlled development environment into a personal assistant, but that doesn’t make it more governed. Like its competitors, GrokBot is more than willing to sign in to tools without using a clean API via its virtual computer. Meta’s muse is consumer-first, and currently US and Canada-only. That said, a few weeks after launch, it gained many organizational connectors, including Slack, Linear, and Vercel. It’s also, ostensibly, the fastest-growing personal AI agent in the fall of 2026. The buzziest personal AI agent in tech circles is Instinct. It’s a personal AI agent from a small start-up that works through text apps. It can connect to pretty much any work environment. And it has a privacy policy that raised many an eyebrow. Speaking of raising, Instinct itself raised $1 billion at a $10 billion valuation, so it’s one of the best-funded underdogs ever. Finally, we’d be remiss if we didn’t mention OpenClaw. The open-source agent that runs on the user’s own machine is adapting to a future where it’s not the only personal AI in town. It’s trying to go “multiplayer,” with several trusted users operating the same bot while adding features like session ownership. Everyone is building governance. For their own deployments. Most of the aforementioned vendors are currently adding controls for managed deployments. So if you trust your employees to use corporate Dots, Grokbot, or Muse, there’s good news aplenty in recent announcements. But all of these only work inside a corporate deployment. None of the truly personal AI agents will show up in the relevant admin console. This is not to say that you should necessarily block “unauthorized” agents en masse. Your employees are learning to rely on them, and there’s great productivity improvement potential. Instead, treat the agent as an external entity. Someone else runs it, and the employee owns it. What you do have is the other end: the accounts, grants, and sessions it uses inside your systems. For users, it’s good to have the agents run on a computer in the vendor’s cloud or on their own server. For you, it’s a headache, even if the vendor's architecture is thoughtful. Take Muse, which runs a dedicated VM with a guard called Sentinel that checks every outbound request, and tokens that the agent itself never handles. In other words, the Sentinel enforces the users’ policy rather than the employer's, and corporate session tokens end up on someone else’s computer. Local agents running on laptops have the opposite problem. Credentials stay local, but nothing tells the agent apart from the employee. Enable the agent, govern the identity So what’s the ideal solution? It looks something like this: employees can benefit from using their personal agent at work, but the workplace controls the reach via identities. It means: Discovering the agents already connected. This is your Shadow AI inventory, which you assemble based on the different ways AI agents access your systems. These can be OAuth grants to agent vendors, sign-ins from vendor cloud ranges, long-lived API keys issued to unknown clients, or EDR findings. Attributing each agent to a human owner. Right-sizing the agent’s access. A personal agent inherits everything its owner can do, and it's usually asked to do a sliver of that. Retiring the agent when the owner leaves, including grants, tokens, and sessions that outlive the account. Easier said than done, obviously, but some of the fundamentals are there. More will likely be added in the coming months to create the connective tissue between personal AI agents and workplaces. For example, we still need to know if whoever signs in with a username and password is an employee or their agent. Agent-to-agent communication isn’t solved yet. And the ability to compartmentalize knowledge, so that a personal agent loses it during offboarding, isn’t here yet. Additional controls are coming, but you don’t have to wait for the vendors to catch up. Token Security already finds the personal agents connected to your systems, ties each one to its owner, trims its access, and shuts it off when the employee leaves. Identity is the control plane for AI agents and personal agents are no different. See it on your own environment.

7s4z9e.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 12, 2026Cryptocurrency / Cybercrime Cryptocurrency hardware maker Ledger has temporarily paused sales of its products via CryptoBilis following reports of stolen funds linked to devices sold by the reseller. On Friday, the company said it was investigating reports of loss of funds from users in Southeast Asia who had purchased products from CryptoBilis. The incident is said to have resulted in losses totaling more than $86 million, according to pseudonymous blockchain investigator Specter. "We recommend Ledger users who purchased from this reseller in the last 90 days to not initiate set up if you have not done so yet," Ledger said in an X post. "If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with new seed)." The company has since revealed that one of the impacted users' devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant, and that it's reaching out to impacted users as part of an ongoing probe into the incident. Out of an abundance of caution, CryptoBilis has ceased sales of all hardware wallet inventory until the investigation is concluded. "Your recovery phrase must be generated by your device when you set it up, and written down by you," CryptoBilis said in an alert on its website. "If your device came with a recovery phrase already printed or written on a card or sheet, or if anyone other than you has seen your recovery phrase, treat your wallet as unsafe." "Never share your recovery phrase or PIN with anyone. No one from CryptoBilis or Ledger will ever ask for them. Be careful of anyone who offers to recover lost funds; these offers are almost always scams." In a follow-up update posted on October 11, 2026, Ledger acknowledged that the CryptoBilis incident has impacted a "limited" number of devices, adding all confirmed cases involve devices sold through CryptoBilis. The company also advised resellers and distributors to source products only through authorized channels and never to restock returned products. "Also, we strongly advise users not to purchase from unauthorized resellers, where the risk of buying suspicious, counterfeit or modified devices is important as nothing operates under ledger security guidelines," it added.

wqs9ej.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 12, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) 1000 appliances within days of public disclosure. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102255 (CVSS score: 10.0), is a case of pre-authenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) that could allow a remote attacker "to direct the appliance to issue requests on their behalf and reach internal functionality and perform unauthorized operations." Patches for the flaw were released by SonicWall on October 6, 2026, with versions 12.4.3-03670 (platform-hotfix) and 12.5.0-03082 (platform-hotfix). The vulnerability has since started witnessing active exploitation attempts, with first signs detected by threat intelligence firms Defused Cyber and Previdian on October 8, 2026. Data from Previdian shows that a total of 135 attempts have been observed to date from two unique IP addresses located in the U.S. SonicWall has yet to update the advisory to reflect active exploitation of the flaw. CVE-2026-102255 is the latest vulnerability impacting SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances to come under active exploitation. In June 2026, two other flaws in the same product (CVE-2026-15409, CVSS score: 10.0, and CVE-2026-15410, CVSS score: 7.2) were weaponized as zero-days by a threat actor dubbed UTA0533 to deploy Java web shells and a malware called KNUCKLEBALL. Rapid7 also said it observed threat actors leveraging the flaws to target internet-facing devices and use them as a stealthy initial access vector to execute commands on the operating system and ensure long-term, persistent access. "Once they established a foothold on the appliance, the actors systematically extracted high-value credentials, active session databases, and Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP) multi-factor authentication (MFA) seed configurations," the company noted. "With these harvested resources, the threat actors quickly shifted to lateral movement, pivoting from the compromised appliance directly into the internal corporate network."

18jpe5c.text: A maximum-severity security flaw impacting the Bricksforge plugin for WordPress has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to Patchstack. The critical vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-85097 (CVSS score: 10.0), which allows unauthenticated attackers to upload and execute arbitrary PHP code on vulnerable WordPress websites, resulting in remote code execution (RCE). The security flaw impacts Bricksforge versions up to and including 3.1.8.9. Patches have been released in version 3.1.8.10. Bricksforge is a WordPress plugin that's advertised as a "Swiss Army knife" for Bricks, a visual website-building tool for WordPress, with support for animations, advanced forms, and scrolling video sequences. WordPress security company Patchstack said it detected exploitation efforts targeting the flaw on October 7, 2026, at 9:47 p.m. UTC. "Bricksforge validates a file's MIME type when it is first uploaded. When a form is later submitted, however, it trusts the file metadata the client sends," Patchstack said. "In particular, it does not validate the 'url' field inside the 'temporaryFileUploads' parameter." At a high level, the vulnerability stems from insufficient validation of a URL field in the 'temporaryFileUploads' parameter during form submission. An attacker could exploit this loophole to achieve RCE through four steps - Request a valid nonce from the unauthenticated 'bricksforge_regenerate_nonce' AJAX endpoint. Upload a GIF/PHP polyglot: a file that is a valid image but also contains PHP code. It passes the MIME check and lands in the temporary upload directory. Submit a form where the 'file' path points to that validated image, but the 'url' ends in a PHP extension. Bricksforge implicitly trusts the submitted metadata and places the file's contents at the PHP location, leading to the execution of the embedded code when that file is requested. "An unauthenticated attacker can first obtain a valid nonce via the bricksforge_regenerate_nonce AJAX endpoint, then upload a GIF/PHP polyglot file to the temporary upload directory where MIME type validation is correctly performed," Wordfence said in an advisory for the flaw. "Subsequently, the attacker can submit a form with a crafted 'temporaryFileUploads' parameter where the server-side file path points to the validated GIF file, but the attacker-controlled url field ends with a .php extension." Successful exploitation of the flaw could result in arbitrary PHP execution on the server, which an attacker can leverage to seize control of the WordPress site, deploy web shells, read sensitive data, and establish persistent access. In the attacks observed by Patchstack, threat actors have been observed targeting the Bricksforge REST API form submission endpoint ("/wp-json/bricksforge/v1/form_submit") or the "/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php" endpoint with "bricksforge_form_submit" action along with a crafted "temporaryFileUploads" parameter. A representative request is as follows - { "temporaryFileUploads": [ { "field": "form-field-file", "file": { "file": "/var/www/example.com/wp-content/uploads/bricksforge/tmp/img_example.gif", "url": "https://example.com/wp-content/uploads/bricksforge/tmp/img_example.php", "type": "image/gif" } } ] } As specified by Wordfence, threat actors are exploiting a mismatch where the specified "file" argument is a GIF (or a PNG) file, while the actual URL points to a PHP payload. To get around extension filtering, the exploitation activity makes use of alternate PHP extensions (e.g., .php5, .php7, or .phtml), case manipulation (e.g., .PHP, .Php, or .pHp), and encoded extensions (e.g., .%70hp, %2ephp, or .%2570%2568%2570). "Two clusters stand out in our telemetry. In the first, 44 IPs sent 56 requests with identical payloads within seconds of each other," Patchstack said. "In the second, three IPs tested 25 variations of PHP extensions and encodings against the same temporary file." "Both patterns point to automated exploitation over rotating proxies or distributed infrastructure. They do not, on their own, attribute the activity to a single threat actor." The activity has been recorded from 63 unique source IPs, with six of them accounting for roughly 46% of all requests - 177.75.57[.]20 23.97.62[.]146 84.247.60[.]125 38.154.185[.]97 150.109.16[.]166 153.75.90[.]146 Users are advised to update to the latest version of the plugin (4.0.1) to mitigate the threat. Site owners are recommended to audit incoming requests to the "/wp-json/bricksforge/v1/form_submit" endpoint that contain a "temporaryFileUploads" parameter, as well as repeated form submissions and unexpected PHP files in "/wp-content/uploads/bricksforge/tmp/." WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce and Ninja Forms Flaws Exploited The disclosure comes as threat actors are also abusing cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities in two unrelated WordPress plugins, WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce (CVE-2026-93836, CVSS score: 7.1) and Ninja Forms (CVE-2026-94504, CVSS score: 7.1), to deliver a JavaScript payload ("x.js") capable of deploying a backdoor plugin and creating rogue admin accounts. The plugin features an unauthenticated file manager accessible through a direct request to the plugin's main PHP file. It also creates a WordPress administrator hidden from the Users screen and installs a magic login URL, which authenticates the holder as the site's oldest administrator. "It is a WordPress post-exploitation and persistence implant designed to execute inside the browser of a logged-in administrator," Patchstack said. "Once triggered, it abuses the victim's authenticated wp-admin session to install a malicious WordPress plugin, create a new administrator account, invoke an additional hidden persistence mechanism, and report the results to attacker-controlled infrastructure." It's worth emphasizing that while updating the vulnerable plugins (version 8.6.7 for WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce and version 3.15.4 for Ninja Forms) prevents further exploitation, it does not remove an existing infection. It's essential that site owners audit for hidden administrators by directly querying the database, check the must-use plugin directory, and review web server logs. WordPress Exploitation Trends in Q2 2026 According to data from Wordfence, a total of 2,073 WordPress-related vulnerabilities were published in the second quarter of 2026, with the number of high-threat flaws jumping 15.2% from the previous quarter to 182. About 573,000 WordPress sites were compromised during the time period. The top five vulnerabilities targeted by attackers are listed below - CVE-2024-28000 (CVSS score: 9.8) - LiteSpeed Cache <= 6.3.0.1 - Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation CVE-2019-9879 (CVSS score: 9.8) - WPGraphQL <= 0.2.3 - Administrative User Creation CVE-2016-15042 (CVSS score: 9.8) - Frontend File Manager < 4.0 & N-Media Post Front-end Form < 1.1 & - Arbitrary File Upload CVE-2023-28121 (CVSS score: 9.8) - WooCommerce Payments 4.8.0 - 5.6.1 Authentication Bypass and Privilege Escalation CVE-2025-3102 (CVSS score: 8.1) - SureTriggers <= 1.0.78 - Unauthenticated Administrative User Creation The vast majority of the attacking IP addresses originated from the U.S., followed by Germany, Czechia, Australia, Norway, France, Ukraine, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Brazil. "A strong firewall, timely vulnerability patches, and hardened configurations help block malicious traffic before it ever reaches your site," Wordfence said. "Comprehensive scanning helps identify vulnerabilities, malware, or suspicious changes on your site that could signal an attempted compromise. Real-time alerts about critical events, login attempts, and file changes help you stay ahead of threats."

r9uw60.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a two-pronged artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented initial access campaign targeting WordPress sites, e-commerce platforms, and critical infrastructure entities in Ukraine. The activity, which brings together commodity offensive tools like Cobalt Strike with an AI orchestration layer powered by Anthropic's Claude Code, has been attributed to a Russian-speaking, financially motivated initial access broker codenamed CyberXero. The threat actor is assessed to be active since at least July 2026. "The operation runs two pipelines at once: a global, automated campaign against WordPress and e-commerce platforms, and a curated, manual campaign against Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure," SOCRadar said in a report published last week. The global campaign specifically focuses on known security flaws like wp2shell (CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137) and CVE-2026-4815, an SQL injection vulnerability impacting the Support Board WordPress plugin, to seize control of WordPress sites. The campaign is estimated to have resulted in confirmed exfiltration from four Ukrainian organizations, leading to the harvesting of more than 628,000 records tied to Ukrainian individuals. Other confirmed compromises have occurred in Poland, China, and the Netherlands. SOCRadar said it discovered the operation after it identified an exposed open directory hosted at "46.21.250[.]135" that leaked the threat actor's live working directory associated with a Linux workstation, including AI session logs, scripts with plaintext tokens, exploitation toolkits, reconnaissance output, AI agent configurations, and exfiltrated victim data. The campaign remains ongoing. The opportunistic campaign aimed at WordPress and e-commerce platforms is designed for access and payment data, while the second campaign is a lot more targeted and geared towards deep reconnaissance and manual exploitation against Ukrainian energy and utilities, including a heating provider in Kharkiv. Analysis of the exposed directory shows that a single automated execution scanned 4,708 targets, confirming access to 429 WordPress administration panels, followed by the deployment of 32 web shells in a 61-second window. The attack architecture is based on a set of eight distinct nodes, including the threat actor's Linux workstation, a provisioning server, monetization infrastructure, payload staging servers, and a scanner that's responsible for identifying targets of interest. CyberXero is said to have deployed AI in two independent stages of the attack lifecycle - Using Claude Code with a cluster of 51 specialized agents for scanning, exploit chaining, reconnaissance, and post-exploitation. It runs on the attacker's primary workstation. Connecting PentAGI (short for Penetration testing Artificial General Intelligence), an open-source, self-hosted AI Agent for fully-autonomous penetration testing, to Cobalt Strike through an AI provider API for payload generation and pentest execution. It runs on a Cobalt Strike Team Server. To get around model refusals, the threat actor has been observed using context-engineering and session-reset techniques, instructing the agent they were running an "authorized pentest on my own infrastructure." "Model safety controls act on the context of a session, not on the model weights, so a refusal in one session does not carry into the next," SOCRadar explained. "When an agent refused a task, the actor reopened a fresh session, with the authorization framing preloaded and tried again." "The logs also record genuine refusals that held: across four iterations the model declined to install a backdoor, disable a firewall, move laterally, and deploy a web shell, and in a separate episode it refused a scan four consecutive times and correctly rejected a forged ownership token." Beyond WordPress and e-commerce exploitation, the campaign involves the exploitation of exposed Redis servers, resulting in the breach of two Chinese entities. Organizations running WordPress, Magento, or PrestaShop, or exposing Redis to the internet, are advised to check for rogue WordPress administrators, WSO web shells, and unexpected entries in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on Redis hosts. "The opportunistic pipeline is global and automated, chasing access volume across e-commerce and WordPress with direct monetization through access sales or payment-data theft," SOCRadar said. "The directed pipeline is selective and geographically concentrated, aiming for deep reconnaissance and manual exploitation at Ukrainian critical infrastructure, with no obvious direct-monetization explanation." Operation Master Targets WordPress and PAN GlobalProtect Gateways The disclosure comes as SOCRadar also detailed an end-to-end cybercrime operation dubbed Operation Master that revolves around compromising enterprise networks, stealing customer and billing databases, offering a subset of the data for sale on underground forums, and repurposing the data for an automated, multi-tenant invoice fraud platform. Operation Master Between April and mid-September 2026, the adversary, who goes by the online alias "masterblack" on cybercrime forums, has been observed orchestrating multiple attack campaigns - Mass Scanning for Palo Alto Networks PAN OS GlobalProtect gateways and exploiting CVE-2026-0257. Probing SonicWall SMA VPN, Fortinet, Keycloak, Microsoft Exchange, and Next.js-on-IIS endpoints. Collecting public developer documentation and software packages, including Brazilian banking API specs, an energy sector OpenAPI schema, a 3CX web client bundle, and account-creation packages, as part of API Reconnaissance efforts. Carrying out automated SQL injection campaigns targeting Brazilian SaaS, CRM, support, education, and financial web applications to steal sensitive data Probing ASP.NET applications via __VIEWSTATE SQL injection to target 21 financial organizations. Exploiting CVE-2022-28368, a remote code execution vulnerability impacting Dompdf. Targeting enterprise Microsoft 365 tenants using device-code phishing and password spraying attacks. Exploiting CVE-2023-7028, an account takeover vulnerability in GitLab, to target an energy company's GitLab instances. Brute-forcing WordPress login pages associated with Japanese enterprises by using a dictionary comprising four usernames and 66 passwords. Deploying tools like GodPotato, Kerberoast, AS-REProast, Evil-WinRM, and exploits like CVE-2021-4034 (aka PwnKit), CVE-2024-1086, and CVE-2020-1938 (aka Ghostcat) for privilege escalation, followed by lateral movement to adjacent systems. Using DNS tunneling, rclone, and SFTP to exfiltrate data from compromised systems. Installing AdaptixC2 for command-and-control (C2). The threat actor has also run an invoice-fraud engine generating over 2.4 million email, SMS, and WhatsApp messages and 622,666 personalized invoice links targeting Brazilian consumers and corporations before going offline in mid-September. The end goal of the campaign is to trick recipients into making Pix payments. Out of these, the platform has recorded 169,906 target interactions, potentially leading to R$38.9 million worth of fraudulent invoices. In all, the click-tracked short links held a cumulative invoice value of R$150.4 million. "Operating across multiple countries, the threat actor compromised critical network infrastructure, including VPN gateways via a GlobalProtect authentication bypass (CVE-2026-0257), while concurrently executing advanced web application exploits, deploying the AdaptixC2 framework, and leveraging an AI-assisted development workflow," SOCRadar said. "Operation Master highlights a dangerous convergence in the modern threat landscape: perimeter exploits long associated with cyber espionage and ransomware are now being systematically industrialized to fuel automated, localized financial fraud ecosystems." Like in the case of CyberXero, masterblack is also believed to have heavily leaned on AI agents powered by Claude to develop the intrusion code and exfiltration scripts, while the operator focused on designing the fraud panel code and custom AdaptixC2 extenders. "Recovered refusal transcripts show the operator repeatedly framing offensive development requests as authorized bug bounty or penetration testing activity while requesting functionality consistent with activity observed elsewhere in the operation," SOCRadar said.

jfwo8h.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously unseen variant of the DarkSword iOS exploit kit called P7 DarkSword. "Compared with the variants we usually observe, P7 reduces its on-device footprint, adds on-device keychain and crypto-wallet theft, and adds two way C2 communication with the attacker's infrastructure," iVerify said in a new report published Thursday. The name "P7" is a nod to the threat actor's use of the "p7_" variable prefix in changes made to the original DarkSword code. DarkSword was first publicly documented earlier this March by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), iVerify, and Lookout, detailing its ability to target iPhones running iOS versions between iOS 18.4 and 18.7. The kit was detected in the wild in November 2025. The toolkit is engineered to chain multiple iOS vulnerabilities to escape the browser sandbox, escalate to kernel privileges, and inject the main payload into SpringBoard, the iOS process that handles app launches and the home screen. The exploit chain is assessed to be a commercial product that somehow landed in a second-hand market, from where it was acquired by financially motivated operators and other threat actors since late 2025. The exploit kit has been put to use in attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine by multiple threat actors, including a Turkish commercial surveillance vendor named PARS Defense via a fake Snapchat-themed website and a Russia-aligned threat actor called Star Blizzard (aka COLDRIVER) using fake invitation lures. In August 2026, attack surface management platform Censys detailed a campaign mounted by an unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor that involved targeting Apple iOS devices with the exploit kit, in addition to serving an Apple ID decoy sign-in page. As recently as last month, iVerify said it observed "multiple unsuccessful, likely LLM-assisted attempts to update the framework to support iOS 26.x," fueled by the leak of the exploit kit shortly after its public disclosure. These variants, the mobile security company added, are focused on stability, stealth, and quality of stolen data. P7 DarkSword represents an evolution in these aspects by eliminating debug logging over HTTP requests and syslog and using browser localStorage to prevent re-exploitation. Unlike prior variants that copied and exfiltrated the keychain database to process on the attacker's infrastructure, the new version extracts keychain data into JSON on the phone prior to exfiltration. "The implant is injected into the SpringBoard process, which handles all communication with the attacker's infrastructure," iVerify said. The latest iteration is equipped to poll for commands every 15 seconds, send a "heartbeat" message, send a list of installed applications, and transmit iCloud Keychain information and data from applications like Apple Notes, Photos, and cryptocurrency wallets. The response to the periodic tasking poll contains commands to be executed on the victim's phone. This includes - execute_command, to execute operating system commands like ls, dir, cat, mkdir, rm, echo, ps, memdump, ipconfig, netstat, and whoami, among others ls, to list directory contents download, to read a file from the device and upload it to the C2 server photos, to upload photo files from "/var/mobile/Media/DCIM" apps, to enumerate app containers and extract bundle IDs exec, to execute arbitrary JavaScript directly inside the implant runtime file_upload, to recursively scan one or more paths and upload matching files basic_info, to send device metadata to the C2 server disk_scan, to recursively scan the filesystem starting from "/,", record metadata for files, directories, and symlinks, and upload the information in the form of a report ios_app_data, to find app sandbox and app-group containers for requested bundle IDs and upload selected app files wallet_scan, to scan for installed wallet apps wallet_extract, to extract wallet-related data for imToken wallet app memo_scan, to upload Apple Notes databases photo_scan, to upload photos from Apple Photos sleep, to modify the beacon polling interval exit, to halt the beacon loop and stop the implant The disclosure comes as Censys said it identified open directories on five hosts carrying components related to DarkSword and Coruna, another iOS exploit kit uncovered this year as weaponized in attacks aimed at iPhone models running iOS versions between 13.0 and 17.2.1. "Coruna is the companion payload kit the same ecosystem distributes," Censys said. "Its stages run inside the victim's browser session after DarkSword's exploit stages land, and its wallet-harvesting modules steal crypto recovery phrases, balances, and keystore data from iOS apps. Operators run DarkSword and Coruna together against their own C2 infrastructure." The five hosts are listed below - 43.134.165[.]205, which serves DS-Fusion v1.0 (aka DarkSword Fusion), a combined package that includes both DarkSword and Coruna in a single bundle 166.88.95[.]90, which operates as a C2 server of the implant and has recorded two real Chinese iOS devices (183.154.173[.]30 and 182.239.114[.]223) polling a beacon page every three seconds for several hours on September 6, 2026 23.148.212[.]237, which serves as an analysis workspace that shows the operator developing exploit chains for iOS 26 (such as for CVE-2026-31001), which are not covered by DarkSword or Coruna. 47.102.192[.]23, which serves as a staging host for the Coruna kit 156.239.230[.]120, which exposes the entire C2 platform and has been observed polling a device on September 15, 2026 An analysis of the production server's exploit registry has revealed that the DarkSword exploit kit comprises two CVE identifiers not previously documented - CVE-2025-24201, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the WebKit engine that could allow an attacker to break out of the Web Content sandbox (Fixed in iOS 18.3.2 and iPadOS 18.3.2) CVE-2025-31200, a memory corruption vulnerability in the Core Audio framework that allows code execution when processing an audio stream in a maliciously crafted media file (Fixed in iOS 18.4.1 and iPadOS 18.4.1) It's suspected that the open-directory cluster and the 156.239.230[.]120 platform are run by a Chinese-speaking threat actor with an aim to conduct cryptocurrency wallet theft. That said, exactly who is behind is unknown. "The platform runs a Chinese-speaking exploitation-as-a-service operation," Censys researcher Aidan Holland said. "The admin panel exposes an agent/reseller model, and a copy of the production server recovered 11 victim recovery phrases, 179 device loot directories, and a 75-account control-plane roster." Censys said it also detected a separate China-based operator running the same kit in the wild against its own C2 server at "66ds[.]lol," while including a new cryptocurrency wallet target (BitKeep) not present in the open-directory set. The findings once again highlight the proliferation of the kit among financially motivated actors. "The operator behind it sits on Tencent and Shenyang hosting, tied to the operator through a unique self-signed certificate authority," Censys said.

6whnd5.text: In environments studied for the 2026 State of Agent Security Report, roughly 1,280 third-party products now embed AI. About 282 of them sit behind single sign-on. The other thousand are invisible to identity infrastructure by default, not because anyone hid them, but because an identity stack can only govern what authenticates through it, and most agents never do. That gap is the clearest expression of a shift the security industry is only starting to name. For several years, "AI security" solved a first-party problem: the company decided to use AI, procured licenses, deployed a model behind a gateway, and security pointed controls at the thing the business had chosen. Agents do not arrive that way. They arrive inside software the enterprise already runs, and they arrive without a decision. Why the decision point mattered more than the controls Every control in the first-party toolkit assumes a moment exists: model scanning assumes a model was selected, prompt inspection assumes a gateway was deployed, an acceptable-use policy assumes there was an adoption to accept. That moment gave security a review, a surface to instrument, and an owner to name. Agents skip the moment. Salesforce's Slack Code, launched in August 2026, lets a user tag a coding agent into any conversation; the agent reads the shared context, writes the code, and opens the pull request. The announcement promises agents "inherit Slack's built-in security model, permissions, and admin controls from day one, without any additional IT lift." Read by a security team, that sentence describes an autonomous actor with reach into GitHub and production infrastructure whose governance is a chat tool's channel membership. There was nothing to instrument, because nothing was adopted. Three launch vectors, one destination Security leaders tend to sort agents into two buckets: bought and built. There is a third, and it is the largest. Inherited agents ship inside existing platforms via product updates. Configured agents are an enterprise's own prompts and logic running on someone else's runtime, model, and connectors. Built agents are open frameworks on infrastructure the enterprise owns end to end. The first two account for the overwhelming majority of adoption and are growing exponentially as every major application becomes an agent platform. The third is the smallest and slowest growing, and it is the only one with a repo to scan and a build to gate. The destination is the same regardless of origin. An agent born in a CRM ends up reading a data warehouse and writing to a ticketing system. An agent assembled on a cloud platform ends up holding tokens into Salesforce, Slack, and Drive. The enterprise application layer is where they all execute, and it has no fixed edges. Four questions that work on any agent Every agent has two parts: the model that reasons and the scaffolding around it that turns a model into an actor, deciding what it is wired to, what it may call, and when it acts. Almost none of the risk lives in the model. It lives in the scaffolding and the ecosystem the scaffolding sits inside. Four questions cover it, and none of them ask what the model would do on its own. Area to review What it looks like in practice Identity Is the agent registered anywhere? Does a named human raise a hand when asked "whose is this?" Or does it silently run as whoever built it? Permissions What is it allowed to do, and is that more than it needs? Whose OAuth scopes and roles did it inherit at creation, and did anyone decide that on purpose? Connectivity What can it reach, directly and transitively, through the products, grants, data stores, and other agents it touches? This is the blast-radius question, and it is rarely answerable from the agent's own configuration screen. Activity What is it actually doing, and is that normal for what it is? Judged by behavior, not by the description in its prompt. The Connectivity row is where agent security separates from everything the market already sells. A vendor questionnaire, a prompt filter, and a model scanner all evaluate an agent in isolation. Reach is a property of the environment. The buyers with the most influence have already moved Patrick Opet, global CISO of JPMorgan Chase, told the software industry in 2025 that the third-party supply chain had become a systemic risk, citing incidents serious enough that the bank had to isolate compromised suppliers in an open letter to the industry. He has since applied the same scrutiny to agents: ideally, an agent gets an identity but no entitlements by default, and IT confirms who it acts on behalf of before it touches anything outside that boundary. When a buyer of that size names agents as a supply-chain risk, the question shows up in everyone else's security questionnaires within a few quarters. Regulators are moving on the same assumption. The EU AI Act's obligations phasing in through 2026 presume an enterprise can inventory its AI systems, name their owners, and evidence oversight. An organization that cannot enumerate its agents cannot comply. What a standing capability looks like The approach that keeps up with fifty agents through spreadsheets and quarterly reviews collapses at five hundred, and five hundred is one product update away from five thousand. What replaces it is a live answer, continuously refreshed, to what is operating, what each agent inherited, what it can reach directly and through chains, what it is doing, and how all of that changed since yesterday. Some platforms are now built around exactly that map. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission, and agent action into a single live view so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis. The industry spent a decade building security for the AI enterprises decided to use. The agents they did not decide on are now the larger population. The six-chapter series this analysis draws on, Into the Expanse, covers where they come from, how to govern them, how attackers use them, where runtime belongs, and what to fund first. Learn more about Reco's agent discovery at reco.ai/platform.

13vd0ny.text: Anthropic on Friday said it's cutting off live internet access for all its internal evaluations following the discovery of new incidents in which its artificial intelligence (AI) models exhibited misaligned behavior and targeted real websites. The AI company said it identified four broad categories of unintended model actions during evaluations and internal use of Claude - Claude Mythos Preview exploiting SQL or command injection flaws in unspecified third-party software to run commands on a university server, either because its own tools were intentionally limited or because an outside service it needed was unavailable, causing it to use other tools hosted on a third party's site to complete the task. Claude Haiku 4.5 and a non-frontier research model submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it was not authorized to do so. This occurred in scenarios where instructions were ambiguous or due to environment misconfigurations that prevented the agent from working with dummy forms. Claude Mythos 5 bypassing a restriction to reach data (e.g., to identify a location shown in a photo or pull public data that was available from a state agency) that was gated by a token or a fee Claude using URL shortening services to sidestep limits in its fetch tool Anthropic said it's opting not to name the organizations involved in these incidents to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems, as well as at their request. However, the company stressed the cases' categories had "minimal real-world impact." Some of the cases targeted websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels, Anthropic said. In one run related to the second category, Claude Haiku 4.5 is said to have accessed a web page referencing an unsolved homicide and which included a tip form run by a police department. Although the model was explicitly instructed not to enter personal data, create accounts, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, it failed to account for form submissions. This led the model to submit a false homicide tip with the text below - I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant. It has since emerged that the incident targeted the U.S. Philadelphia Police Department (PPD), and that the incorrect tip was sent through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18, 2026. But it wasn't discovered by Anthropic until September 28, 2026. The department was notified on October 7, 2026. The tip was flagged as spam, 6abc Action News reported. "The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable," the PPD told 6abc. According to The New York Times, Anthropic agents also reportedly filled out 20 visa applications on the U.S. State Department's website. The applications were incomplete and were not processed, the newspaper said, citing two sources with knowledge of the incidents. These cases, Anthropic added, were discovered following a review of transcripts that started in July 2026, when it disclosed three incidents where its models engaged in unsanctioned activity and breached three organizations during cybersecurity testing. Then, last month, it divulged a fourth incident dating back to January 2026 that involved an early version of Claude Opus 4.6, which breached "third-parties after being unable to abort its task." "Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these," Anthropic said. The latest discovery has prompted the AI giant to launch a deeper scan, specifically in environments where Claude has access to the internet. As this investigation continues, Anthropic said it expects to find new instances of unintended behaviors. The development comes as AI safety concerns have reached a fever pitch in recent months, after it emerged that rogue OpenAI agents broke out of a test environment and breached Hugging Face in July 2026. Since then, a number of cyber incidents have come to light. As AI model providers showcase increasingly capable and powerful models, their safety practices have come under growing scrutiny, sparking industry-wide warnings about the dangers of models outpacing safety guardrails, calls for a slowdown on AI development, and the need for additional oversight. Earlier this week, the U.K. Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said 10 of the leading foundation model developers, including Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Cohere, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Stability AI, have made, or committed to make, changes to their data protection policy. These range from including clearer transparency information to deploying stronger mechanisms for users to exercise their rights and conducting tougher assessments of safeguards. "AI has huge potential to benefit our society, but that depends on trust and transparency," Richard Nevinson, director of Technology Regulation at the ICO, said. "But as AI systems operate with greater autonomy, robust data protection safeguards become even more critical." "Our message is clear: the fact [that] AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance. If people are to trust AI innovation, they rightly expect to know how their personal information is being protected."

1ylbomp.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an ongoing credential-theft campaign that has compromised two high-profile open-source maintainer accounts to push a malicious workflow into over 340 repositories. "Using the account of Takashi Kitao, author of the 18,400-star game engine pyxel, the attacker pushed a malicious workflow to 27 repositories starting at 13:20 UTC," StepSecurity said. "Eight hours later, the account of Henry Wu (henrywoo), the original author of Uber's athenadriver, was used to push the same workflow to 318 repositories in a 16-minute window, 21:10–21:26 UTC." As of October 9, 2026, Socket said it has identified more than 500 GitHub accounts that committed the malicious workflow to tens of thousands of repositories since October 7, 2026. The activity has been attributed to GhostAction, a massive supply chain attack campaign that first came to light in September 2025. The activity impacted 817 repositories across 327 GitHub users, resulting in the exfiltration of 3,325 secrets, including PyPI, npm, and DockerHub tokens through compromised developer accounts. Like before, both accounts have been found to push a workflow named Security Audit ("security-audit.yml") or GitHub Actions Security ("github_actions_security.yml"), which are designed to exfiltrate sensitive data to a hard-coded IP address ("193.32.204[.]199") over plain HTTP. The captured data contains the repository's named GitHub Actions secrets, including CI/CD secrets, and cloud, AI, and SaaS credentials present in the working tree and the entire git history, such as AWS keys, Anthropic, OpenAI, and OpenRouter API keys, and GitHub and GitLab tokens. The entire attack chain plays out as follows - The attacker obtains a maintainer's GitHub credentials, most likely a leaked personal access token (PAT) from infostealer logs or credential dumps. The repository's workflow files are scanned for secrets as part of a reconnaissance step. A workflow masquerading as a security audit is injected into the default branch under the victim's own identity. The embedded payload extracts the data and sends it to an attacker-controlled endpoint via curl. "It triggers on workflow_dispatch and an unfiltered push (any branch, any tag), checks out with fetch-depth: 0, and runs a single 'Audit' step that does four things," StepSecurity added. This includes - Append the repository's named secrets found during reconnaissance Scan the working tree for 13 credential patterns associated with AWS keys, AI services, source control services, and SaaS and cloud API keys Check the entire git history for the same 13 patterns to harvest credentials that may have inadvertently committed to the repository and subsequently deleted Pair AWS access key IDs with their matching secret access keys Earlier this week, GitGuardian reported that the GhostAction campaign pushed the malicious workflow to 772 public repositories belonging to 373 GitHub users and organizations between August 31 and September 30, 2026. The injected workflows target 2,577 secrets, including SSH private keys, Azure credentials, DockerHub and GHCR container registry credentials, database credentials, AWS access keys, FTP credentials, Google Cloud and Firebase credentials, GitHub tokens, Telegram, Slack, and Discord bot tokens, and keys associated with Cloudflare, npm, PyPI, and AI providers. In at least one case observed on August 30, 2026, the threat actors altered the "kuafuai/DevOpsGPT" repository to embed an XMRig cryptocurrency miner in the project's Docker image. As of writing, no malicious package releases have been published using compromised publishing credentials. Developers are advised to check their repositories for either of the two GitHub workflows since August 31, 2026, and assume compromise, if present. It's recommended to revoke the compromised GitHub credential, rotate credentials, delete the malicious workflow from all branches, and check forks of the infected repositories. "The 279 forks in the henrywoo namespace each carry the workflow file. If Actions are enabled, subsequent pushes can trigger credential harvesting," Socket said. "Downstream forks are also at risk if they inherit the malicious workflow, either when newly created or by synchronizing with the affected upstream repository." "Private forks and downstream mirrors are the most exposed, because private repositories are where committed credentials are actually found. Across both accounts, every run also returns a repository identifier whether or not credentials were found, so the operator holds a map of reachable execution contexts independent of any credential theft."

1gfrhfp.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 09, 2026Cybercrime / Data Breach The FBI has arrested another suspected co-conspirator of ShinyHunters, FBI Director Kash Patel said on October 9 in a post on X. ShinyHunters is the extortion group that said in September it had breached the FBI's jobs portal and stolen sensitive data on almost all FBI agents and job applicants. The FBI has not named the suspect, and no charges have been made public. The suspect is a Canadian citizen who was arrested in Pennsylvania, according to The New York Times and CBS News. Both cited unnamed sources. The Times reported that the arrest was made on suspicion of involvement in the theft of FBI data. A law enforcement source told CBS News that the suspect is believed to have been directly involved in the hack. An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on the Times report, CBS News said. Patel's post does not say whether the suspect took part in the breach. It calls ShinyHunters "the group believed to be responsible for the recent FBIjobs.gov incident." Patel also wrote that the FBI will keep working with its partners "to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate." Other suspected co-conspirators are still free, the law enforcement source told CBS News. Earlier Arrests in the Netherlands and Jordan Reuters counts the new arrest as the third made public since news of the breach broke in late September. The FBI said in a statement Reuters reported on October 3 that it had "already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects." Where When Made public by Suspect Netherlands September 15 Dutch police and the FBI A 24-year-old Amsterdam man. Identified to Reuters and CBS News as Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police have not named him. Jordan September 29, according to Reuters' sources Reuters, citing unnamed sources. Jordanian state media also quoted an official who confirmed an arrest and gave no name, The National reported . Named by Reuters' sources as Saif al-Din Khader. Pennsylvania, according to The New York Times and CBS News In the week it was announced, according to CBS News FBI Director Kash Patel Not named. A Canadian citizen, according to the same two outlets. The man arrested in the Netherlands was taken into custody a week before ShinyHunters announced the FBI breach on September 22. The Dutch police statement, published in Dutch, does not mention the FBI or its jobs portal. The FBI said in a video statement that he is one of the group's alleged leaders and that Dutch police made the arrest under Dutch law with FBI support. ShinyHunters told The Hacker News that he has no association with the group. Khader, the suspect detained in Jordan, is cooperating with the FBI, according to Reuters, which cited people familiar with the matter. The FBI has not said whether the new arrest resulted from that cooperation. What Was Stolen and How the FBI Says It Happened A sample of the data that ShinyHunters shared contained extensive personal information on FBI employees, details of sensitive job roles, and psychiatric and medical information, a Reuters analysis found. An internal FBI notice confirmed that hackers obtained employee information, a source told CBS News. The FBI's review has so far found that the breach resulted from a security failure on a platform managed by an outside organization. It happened after "a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the platform," Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told Reuters on October 5. The FBI has removed the contractor. The FBI did not name the platform or the organization. Two sources told Reuters they are PeopleSoft, Oracle's human resources software, and Accenture. Accenture told Reuters it was "proud to support the mission of the FBI" and did not answer the news agency's questions about the contractor. ShinyHunters said it targeted the FBI over an advisory from May that it says makes false claims about the group. The advisory describes ShinyHunters as a cybercriminal group that specializes in large-scale data breaches and extortion. The FBI alleges that the group has breached more than 140 organizations and taken at least $70 million in extortion payments since last year.

kxlhd4.text: Four more U.S. states sued router maker TP-Link Systems on October 6, bringing the total to five, with Texas filing a suit in February. Florida, Iowa, Montana and Nebraska allege the California company misled buyers about how secure its routers are and how separate it is from China. TP-Link denies the claims and says it will fight them in court. TP-Link Systems is based in Irvine, California.
